essay:the-theology-of-time.title: What Does the Bible Say About Time Management?
essay:the-theology-of-time.notes: This is the old register with nothing else in it: 272 words in nineteen paragraphs, most of them one sentence, with two runs of three-plus one-sentence paragraphs ("The Son of God operated with limits. / And He did not apologize for them. / The question is not whether your life is full. / The question is whether your life is faithful.") and five "Not X. Y." turns carrying the whole argument. Nothing accumulates: no familiar account conceded, no opposing case, no history, and "Sabbath came before the fall" is asserted rather than shown. The single "we" ("Even Christians have baptized this lie") never reaches "I"; the ending ("sacrificing what is eternal on the altar of what feels urgent") is a slogan restating the opening. The thinking (efficiency as waste, limits without apology) is sound and worth an essay, so rewrite rather than cut; note also that "redeem the time" is KJV phrasing for Ephesians 5:16 (ESV: "making the best use of the time"), and the source body carries literal "\n\n" escapes that suggest a data-import problem.

signals.thesis: Time management is not the deepest problem; worship is, because until you know what your time is for, efficiency wastes it as surely as laziness.
stockPhrases: baptized this lie
on the altar of what feels urgent
unverifiable: "redeem the time" is attributed to Paul in Ephesians 5 but is KJV wording, not the site's ESV default

essay:culture-discipleship-not-attendanc.title: What a Church Counts Is What a Church Becomes
essay:culture-discipleship-not-attendanc.notes: Accumulates the way the standard asks: confession first ("I can count a sanctuary from a pulpit without anyone catching me at it"), Goodhart's mechanism conceded and then taken underneath by David's census ("Same arithmetic. Different sin."), Christendom and Finney's anxious bench for the history, and a steelman the counters would sign ("only a fool refuses to take a pulse") before the verdict. The writer stays inside the indictment to the end ("more Sundays than I want to write down, as a king counting swords"; "I still count the room"). Scripture is verbatim ESV and governs the argument; Goodhart/Strathern 1975/1997, Finney 1835, Bonhoeffer 1937/1945, Willard 2006 all match what I know, though checked from memory rather than primary text. Roughly seven "Not X. Y." turns across eight movements sits at the standard's limit, and the em-dash avoidance has left comma splices that need a copyedit ("It was a joke with a warning folded inside, a church can count its money and its heads"; "the pastor, I am done pointing away from myself, the pastor gets to be necessary"). Ending earned: Paul "wrote the sentence and died, and the sentence came true."

signals.thesis: Attendance is the floor of the Christian life and the church made it the ceiling; a church becomes what it counts, and Scripture counts generations, not gatherings.

essay:bivocational-pastors-get-right.title: What Bivocational Pastors Get Right
essay:bivocational-pastors-get-right.notes: The argument is real and the steelman is honest ("Commanded. The salaried pastorate is no corruption of the apostolic pattern"; "If a church can free such a man for the word and will not, the shame belongs to the church"), and the self-implication is specific ("I am translating his fear rather than remembering my own"). But the back half runs on the old gait: nine "Not X. Y." constructions ("not a rough patch... It was a settled practice"; "has not discovered the apostolic pattern. It has discovered a discount"; "not the junior varsity... he is the varsity"; "not a fallback. It is the oldest shape"; "he did not show them a credential. He showed them his hands"), fragment punches standing in for sentences ("These hands." "Night and day." "Commanded."), a section titled "Not junior varsity," and a three-address close ("So to the churches... And to the networks... And to the man himself") that is sermon architecture. Scripture verbatim and doing work. The parked-truck freight driver reads as a specific man and should be confirmed as real or marked as a composite. The final line ("So was the man who made tents") is earned; the run-up to it needs to be prose.

signals.thesis: The bivocational pastorate is the oldest and most common shape of the office, not a rough draft of it; the salaried norm is a modern professional drift and the ranking it produced should die.
stockPhrases: Listen to how we speak about him.
unverifiable: Opening anecdote of the freight-company driver writing his sermon in a parked truck: real person or composite is not indicated

essay:return-ministry-after-burnout.title: How Do You Return to Ministry After Burnout?
essay:return-ministry-after-burnout.notes: The pastoral substance is the strongest in the batch and the self-implication is real ("I have asked a brother on leave, 'So when are you coming back?'... it was a deadline wearing encouragement's clothes"), the Elijah and Peter readings stay with the text long enough to do theological work, and the "door marked not going back" section says the sentence nobody says. But the register is the old one: roughly fourteen "Not X. Y." constructions ("is not the collapse. It is the first good week afterward"; "is not faithfulness; it is relapse with a liturgy"; "Rest is not the concession... It is the instruction"; "The pedestal is not a gift. It is the old job description, gilded"; "Not the ministry. The soul."), one-word paragraph leads that are sermon outline ("Patience." "Honesty." "No pedestal."), and a final paragraph built on anaphora that recaps the three Scripture sections ("Elijah got bread before... Peter got breakfast before... The apostles got the boat before") and then ends on a fragment stack. The "(ESV)" tag after every one of some twenty citations is decoration. Scripture itself is verbatim and accurate. The fix is targeted: cut two-thirds of the antitheses, dissolve the one-word leads into paragraphs, and end on the Psalm 23 paragraph, which already carries the weight.

signals.thesis: Returning after burnout is not a re-entry but a different life inside the same vocation, and God restores worn-out servants in a fixed order: fed first, asked second, sent third, never alone.
stockPhrases: wearing encouragement's clothes
relapse with a liturgy
the old job description, gilded

essay:pastors-depression-not-faith-probl.title: Is a Pastor's Depression a Faith Problem?
essay:pastors-depression-not-faith-probl.notes: Does the mature architecture honestly: the folk doctrine gets its strongest form with its own Scripture ("They are holding half of the truth with both hands"), the distinction that changes things is creation not therapy ("a quiet denial of the doctrine of creation"), the history is named (revivalism, prosperity teaching, professionalization), and the writer is inside it first ("That was not integrity. It was fluency"; "I did it for longer than I will write down"). Scripture is verbatim ESV and governing across Elijah, Jeremiah, David, Psalm 88, and 2 Corinthians 1; Spurgeon's "The Minister's Fainting Fits" and John of the Cross on melancholy are real. Crisis care is exemplary: 988, "that thought is a symptom, not a fact," "I am a pastor, not a clinician." Antithesis density (about eleven) trends high for the standard, and the quip "heaven has been hiring wrong since Sinai" and the triple "No rebuke. No sermon. Sleep, first." are the lines to trim; "the largest congregation on earth" for Spurgeon's Tabernacle should be softened to "among the largest." Ending earned and passes through mercy: "God did not ask his servant to be stronger. He fed him. He has not changed."

signals.thesis: A pastor's depression is not a faith problem; the folk doctrine that a depressed shepherd is a disqualified shepherd cannot survive the Bible it claims to defend.
stockPhrases: unbelief wearing a medical alias
heaven has been hiring wrong since Sinai
unverifiable: "the largest congregation on earth" (Spurgeon's Metropolitan Tabernacle) is overstated; "one of the largest" is what I can support

essay:small-churches-get-right.title: What Small Churches Get Right
essay:small-churches-get-right.notes: The steelman is the best in the batch and would be signed by its defenders ("The crowd was her convalescent ward. Some people are standing in the faith today because a big room let them lie down in it first"), and the writer refuses the cheap move by name ("The pastor of a large church is not, by that fact, the hired hand of verse twelve"). History is concrete (McGavran 1965/1970, Dunbar early 1990s, Bonhoeffer's Finkenwalde, Peterson's twenty-nine years in Bel Air), and the Matthew 18:20 reading in context is the essay's real gift, turning a consolation prize into a commission. Self-implication is honest without theater ("I never learned to stop comparing"). About six "Not X. Y." turns, each at a hinge; no fragment stacks; ending returns to the driveway and is earned ("It is whether you know theirs"). One small inaccuracy: Zechariah 4:10 is called "the question" a pastor should tape inside his pulpit, but the ESV quoted is a declaration (the question form is KJV).

essay:gen-z-wants-from-church.title: What Does Gen Z Actually Want From Church?
essay:gen-z-wants-from-church.notes: The thinking is sound, the attractional church gets a genuine steelman ("missionaries who read their field correctly, and the criticism that follows means nothing without that sentence"), the rich young ruler is read with care ("The cost was what the love looked like once it took the man seriously"), and the self-implication is specific ("I shortened sermons that needed their length... I lost the room anyway"). But the essay is built as a four-point outline whose headings are themselves parallel antitheses ("They will forgive uncertainty. They will never forgive spin." / "They have algorithms. They need elders."), each section closing on a manufactured slogan ("They are not afraid of hard. They are bored of easy."; "The volume is the deficiency."; "Children do not inherit our marketing. They inherit our actual gods."), roughly ten "Not X. Y." turns, and a stock turn on the explicit avoid list ("sit with that"). The standard asks for one memorable verdict earned by the argument over several attempted slogans; this has a slogan per paragraph. "Older men who let me stand close enough to watch them live" extends the known biography and should be confirmed with James. Fix: keep the argument and the ending, dissolve the four-part scaffold into accumulation, keep two slogans.

signals.thesis: The young are not leaving because the church demanded too much of them but because they suspect it was never going to demand anything; raised inside the ad, they want honesty over spin, depth over content, elders over algorithms, and cost over ease.

say that plainly, because it is true
He always finds the seam.
unverifiable: "what pulled me was not programming... It was older men who let me stand close enough to watch them live" extends the conversion biography beyond the facts on file

essay:reformed-charismatic-pastors-same-.title: Can Reformed and Charismatic Pastors Work Together?
essay:reformed-charismatic-pastors-same-.notes: This is the contested-doctrine method executed as written: the weak cessationist reading is retired before the strong one is built ("Face to face. Fully known. That is not the arrival of a book"), the continuationist gets the counterpunch and the global church ("Seen from Lagos or São Paulo, the gifts did not cease. They moved"), the order of the question is named before the verdict, and the self-implication goes further than any other piece in the batch, naming the objection he cannot answer ("A door held ajar that no one is ever welcomed through functions like a wall with better manners, and I am not certain mine is more than that"). Azusa 1906, Warfield 1918, Bennett 1960, Duquesne 1967, Strange Fire 2013, Grudem 1988, Carson 1987, the Pew 2011 quarter, and the 1689 Confession's "being now ceased" all match what I know; Scripture is verbatim ESV. Only about five "Not X. Y." turns, all at hinges; the ending passes through 1 Corinthians 13 and is earned. The pass is contingent on one thing only James can confirm: the essay's whole "Where I land" section rests on his being a 1689 Reformed Baptist, which is not among the biographical facts on file. If that is not his confession, that section is invented biography and the piece drops to revise.

signals.thesis: The gifts are a second-order question that divides faithful churches but not the faith; the debate keeps drowning out the first-order question of whether you will sit down at the table with the other man.

essay:global-south-church-teach-sufferin.title: What Does the Global Church Know About Suffering?
essay:global-south-church-teach-sufferin.notes: The thinking and architecture are sound: prayer-list opener, Jenkins, Constantine to the postwar suburbs, Smith and Denton's moralistic therapeutic deism doing real work, Luther's Thesis 21 quoted accurately, and a genuine steelman ("The comfortable church is not simply wrong"; 1 Timothy 2:2 as the argument against the writer). The failure is register density: eleven 'Not X. Y.' constructions in 2,277 words ("The error was never the comfort. The error is the theology"; "is not courage as a personality trait. It is a settled..."; "is not a specialty tool... It is the ordinary theology"), which is roughly two per movement and turns the hinge into the gait; the standard says to mark that revise. The close is a three-beat fragment stack in the old voice ("They found out early. We will find out late. But we will find out."), and "No one prints it on a mug" is a quip the calm register does not need. Self-implication is strong ("I have preached the hard texts softly because the room was grieving and I flinched"), and the writer's refusal to invent field anecdotes ("I will not decorate them with invented stories") is exactly right. Fix: thin the antitheses to the three or four that carry weight, let the last paragraph end on the sentence about God not being absent rather than the tricolon.

signals.thesis: The American church promoted comfort from mercy to covenant, so suffering reads as breach of contract; the global South's unsurprised theology of the cross is not a specialty tool but the ordinary Christian theology we misplaced during the long peace.

Self-implication is specific ("I have approved the mailers and argued about the font"). What holds it at revise is the fabrication gate, not the prose: the ending rests on a detailed conversion narrative with quoted dialogue ("The Christian who finally cracked my settled unbelief... said, more than once, *that is a real question*"; "People fed me... a long stretch of time, no ask at the end") that extends the known biography into exactly the kind of story the audit warns "sounds right." It must be confirmed by James or the essay rewritten around the hole. Secondary: the close runs a triple anaphora ("Anyone unhurried enough... Anyone settled enough... Anyone who can say") and ends on two fragments ("Not the death of their belief. The exhaustion of ours."), old-register moves stacked where one would land.

signals.thesis: The unaffiliated cannot be marketed to because their defining trait is that they stopped believing the marketing; what reaches them is slow, personal, unhurried presence, which the writer knows because it is what reached him.

essay:ai-authenticity-pastor-artificial-.title: If AI Can Write a Sermon, What Is a Pastor For?
essay:ai-authenticity-pastor-artificial-.notes: The argument is genuinely excellent and the history is real and specific (the Phaedrus, Hugh of Saint-Cher's concordance c. 1230, Cruden 1737, Strong 1890, radio in 1921), the fear is given "its strongest form, not its silliest" before the line is redrawn through the man, and Ezekiel 3 is allowed to do sustained theological work rather than serve as an epigraph. Self-implication is precise ("I have twenty-one books and a platform with my name on it, more reason than most to want the producing made easier"). Two things keep it from passing. First, John 10:5 is misquoted: the essay prints "for they do not know his voice" where the ESV reads "for they do not know the voice of strangers," and it is labeled ESV; that has to be corrected. Second, antithesis is the default connector at eleven hard-period turns ("Delivery was never the office. Ingestion was."; "Openness is not a courtesy... It is the load-bearing wall"; "Integrity does not have a technology problem. It has only ever had a truth-telling problem"), with the 2 Corinthians 4 paragraph carrying three in a row. The ending is earned ("The machine can produce everything about a sermon except a man who was there"), and the fix is a thinning pass, not a rebuild.

signals.thesis: The machine did not change the pastoral office; it changed the price of the counterfeit, and the one thing it cannot do is eat the scroll for you, so the test is whether a pastor could describe from the pulpit what he did in the study.

essay:17-mobilizing-your-church-for-worl.title: How Can a Church Do World Missions on a Small Budget?
essay:17-mobilizing-your-church-for-worl.notes: Leaving this up costs trust on every axis at once. A reader arriving from search for the missions topic gets a burnout article with unrendered "\n\n" markers and dropped apostrophes ("other peoples grief", "Its about structure", "a pastors inner life"). The prose is the old fragment register and generic to the point of anonymity ("Not to shame you back into your role. Not to lecture you about commitment. But to name what is actually happening"; "You're still performing. You're still producing. But something essential has gone dark inside."), with no self-implication (the writer addresses "you" from outside) and a closing that is generic hope plus an institutional pitch ("The calling you carry is worth fighting for, and so are you"; "The Pastors Connection Network was built precisely for this"). It also prints a debunked statistic as fact: "anywhere from 1,500 to 1,700 pastors quit ministry every month" — Lifeway Research has repeatedly shown the figure is near 250 and that the higher numbers have no traceable source, and "Research from Barna Group consistently shows" cites nothing. The two quoted pull-lines are the article quoting itself. Unpublish this unit; if James wants the missions-on-a-small-budget piece, it must be written from scratch, and the burnout piece, if kept anywhere, needs its own slug, the statistic removed, and a full rewrite.

essay:where-church-was-silent.title: Where the Church Was Silent
essay:where-church-was-silent.notes: The fairness and self-implication are exemplary: the indictment is given "its full weight before I dare to answer it," the writer's own convention is named first ("I preach in a house whose foundation was poured over that grave"), and the Nathan turn is executed honestly ("It is the Pharisee's prayer with the dates updated"). Every historical claim checked out: Augusta 1845, the 1995 resolution, Whitefield and Georgia, King's April 1963 letter to eight clergymen with both quotations verbatim, the Globe in 2002, the 2022 Guidepost findings, Douglass's 1845 appendix line, and FBC Fenton is in fact an SBC church, so "My tribe. My name on the door" is true biography. What holds it at revise is register: twelve hard-period antitheses ("The hardest case against Christianity is not a syllogism. It is a record."; "This is not the enemy's history. It is the family history."; "Not at the skeptic's house. At ours.") plus three anaphoric triplets ("It is the record of... It is the record of... It is the record of"; "It cried from... It cried from... It has been crying"; "not like those churchmen... not like the moderates... not like the bishops"), and a signpost ("Here is where the honest skeptic and the honest believer part"). Each move is executed well, which is exactly the case the standard names as still failing the mature register. One citation splice: Ezekiel 34:4 is elided to "... but with force and harshness" where the ESV reads "and with force and harshness." The ending passes through confession and is fully earned ("guilty. Lord, have mercy. We heard, and we said nothing.").

signals.thesis: The church's record of silence on slavery, segregation, and abuse is the honest skeptic's strongest case, and the standard that judged it was Scripture's own prophetic word, which means the reckoning cannot end with the dead but must begin with the writer's own church and its silences it cannot yet see.
stockPhrases: Here is where the honest skeptic and the honest believer part
unverifiable: Ezekiel 34:4 elided with "... but with force and harshness you have ruled them" — ESV reads "and with force and harshness"; the ellipsis alters a conjunction inside a marked quotation

essay:justice-not-political-theological.title: Is Justice a Political Issue or a Theological One?
essay:justice-not-political-theological.notes: The argument is sound and the Scripture is accurate and load-bearing (Genesis 18:19, Jeremiah 22:16, Psalm 82:3–4, Deuteronomy 24, Micah 6:8, all ESV-correct with references), the steelmans are real ("The progressive reading is not a smuggled cargo"; "The conservative reading is not paranoia either"), and the fatherless paragraph is the true biography doing exactly the work the voice asks for ("That is not a political position I hold. It is a debt I owe."). But this is the most antithesis-dependent essay in the set: fifteen or more hard-period 'not X, it is Y' turns in 2,179 words ("Doing justice for the poor is not the application of knowing God. It is knowing God."; "The water Amos wants is not a movement. It is the character of God"; "The recovery is not a moderate position... It is underneath them"), closing on a fragment pair ("Not as a slogan. As the character of the God who noticed him"). The structure is also perfectly symmetrical by design ("The left keeps the structure and loses the heart. The right keeps the heart and loses the structure"; "Capture and evasion are the same error wearing opposite jerseys"), which the standard flags both as a machine tell and as a false-balance risk; the essay asserts equal responsibility without arguing it. Signposts ("Here is what undoes them both"; "Read it slowly"; "See what that does to our categories") should go. Keller's "quartet of the vulnerable" is real (Generous Justice). Ending is earned through confession ("I have used this word as a team color").

signals.thesis: Justice (mishpat u-tsedaqah) is God's own character before it is any party's program, and each political tribe kept half the biblical word, threw the other half away, and accused its rival of the theft it had committed.

essay:poor-not-ministry-category.title: What Does the Bible Say About the Church and the Poor?
essay:poor-not-ministry-category.notes: Of the eight, this is the essay closest to the mature voice in architecture and posture: the binder opener is concrete, the steelman is given by a man who is one of its defenders ("Whoever wants to sneer at structure will have to begin by sneering at the apostles"), the James 2 paragraph is a long cumulative reading that stays with the text, the Matthew 25 crux is handled honestly ("Commentators divide honestly over 'these my brothers'... I will not pretend the question away"), and Julian's 362 letter is explicitly marked as paraphrase. Self-implication is the best in the set ("The committee did its job faithfully. I used its faithfulness as my alibi"; "I have given a man who smelled like the weather warm directions to an agency across town"). It sits at revise rather than pass on register density alone: twelve hard-period antitheses ("The seating chart is not hospitality logistics. It is a confession of faith."; "The structure was never the sin. The filing-away was."; "They did not refuse Christ; they filed him."), which is one per paragraph rather than one per movement. Keep the three or four that land (the last two above earn their place) and convert the rest to developed sentences. The atheist-auditor persona ("Before I believed in God I believed in ledgers") is a modest extension of known biography and reads as true; the ending is earned and passes through Christ in the poor man's skin ("someone we claim to worship was standing inside his skin. And still is.").

signals.thesis: Scripture has no mercy category; the poor are a test administered to the whole church at the door, and the committee's faithfulness became the writer's alibi for filing away what God never intended to be filed.

essay:creation-care-not-optional.title: What Does Genesis Say About Caring for Creation?
essay:creation-care-not-optional.notes: The argument accumulates properly: the fearful man in the pew is honored before he is answered ("He is not a fool for declining to convert"), the green altar gets "the same instrument," Lynn White is conceded before he is corrected, and the ending passes through the empty tomb to the five sons ("The second one is still in the sentence") and earns its weight. Every citation checks: Schaeffer 1970, White in Science 1967, the abad/shamar link to Numbers 3:7-8, the 2 Peter 3:10 'found' reading, Wright 2008, Flint 2014, and all ESV quotations verbatim. What keeps it from shipping as it stands is register: the eschatology section stacks five antitheses in two paragraphs ("Renewal, not replacement." "Childbirth, not a death rattle." "all things made new, not all new things made" "does not end with an evacuation. It ends with an arrival"), the Settled/Unsettled pair is engineered symmetry, "Nineteen seventy." is a one-word fragment for effect, and "White got the symptom right... He got the anthropology wrong" is the CLAUDE.md template verdict verbatim. Em-dash stripping has also left comma splices a reader trips on ("for their own appetite, Ezekiel's entire indictment"; "a lifeboat, D. L. Moody said nearly that"). Trims, not a rebuild.

signals.thesis: The church surrendered the doctrine of creation to the political tribes rather than losing it in argument; Genesis 2:15's two verbs, dominion as answerable kingship, creation's groan, and an eschatology of renewal rather than evacuation bind Christians to keep the earth while leaving the mechanisms open.

essay:individual-sin-systemic-sin-2.notes: This is the essay in the batch I would defend line by line. It does what the standard asks: both positions at full strength before any verdict ("the weak versions have taught nobody anything"), the first/second-order sorting stated before arguing, the writer's landing named with its lineage ("the covenantal reading... the federal theology of the Reformed confessions"), and a section titled "The objection I have not answered" that concedes "The other side is holding a real card. An editor would trim two or three of the nine antitheses ("It is the canon. You are not straddling a fence. You are standing where Daniel stood" is three verdicts in a row) and fix the comma splice at "into anesthesia, our fathers did this," but the paragraphs are developed and the verdicts sit at hinges.

essay:disability-justice-theological.notes: The objection is steelmanned and conceded ("Nearly all of that is true, and none of it gets walked back here"), and the turn is precise: "We took a real hope and made it a schedule. Healing became the thing that happens before full membership." One quotation is not verbatim: the essay gives John 9:3 as "It was not this man who sinned, or his parents" where the ESV reads "It was not that this man sinned, or his parents." It is serious and biblical, and the half of the church that waves it away with a chant has not answered it.' / 'That case is also serious, also biblical. The 'Not X. Y.' gait runs about seven hard-period instances plus a half-dozen inline antitheses ('A hermeneutic that always lands on the side of your own comfort is not a hermeneutic. It is a mirror.'), thickest in the indictment and 'What is bound' sections. Fix: let the two steelmans differ in length and shape, cut the twin closers and the foreshadowing line 'Hold that distinction; it will indict both rooms before this essay ends', and thin the verdicts to one per movement. The fatherless-at-the-gate paragraph and the five-sons paragraph are the essay's real voice and should carry more of it.

essay:reformation-actually-about.title: What the Reformation Was Actually About
essay:reformation-actually-about.notes: This is the model for how the corpus should handle history. It moves from the familiar account (the foam hammer) through what is true in it, into Luther's Anfechtung, and it audits its own legends in public: the door 'enters the record only after Luther's death' via Melanchthon, Iserloh 1961, 'Here I stand' in printed accounts rather than the transcript, Foxe's ploughboy marked as 'a secondhand report'. Every date I checked holds (Stotternheim July 1505, first mass 1507, the 1545 preface, September 1522, Tyndale 1536, Manz January 1527, Marburg 1529, Augsburg 1555, Trent's justification decree 1547, Pius V 1567, van Lodenstein 1674). Rome gets its strongest voice and the writer names the objection he cannot answer (John 17:21: 'It is a conviction I can defend. It is not one I can celebrate.'). Self-implication is specific ('My family tree contains the drowned man and the men on the bank', 'The twenty-seventh thesis has my name in it somewhere'). Five 'Not X. Y.' constructions across seven sections, no fragment stacks, contractions absent but the prose reads spoken. The one soft spot is the final three fragments ('Reformed, and always being reformed. The reforming is not done. This time it starts with us.'), a slogan tail on a paragraph that had already landed; I would still defend it as a hinge.

signals.thesis: The Reformation was neither the hero story nor the fraud story but one terrified conscience finding a gracious God in Romans 1:17, and its heirs must own both the recovered gospel and the graves it dug.

essay:truth-in-post-truth-world.title: How Does the Church Tell the Truth in a Post-Truth Age?
essay:truth-in-post-truth-world.notes: Architecture and fairness are in voice: the postmodern critique is conceded generously ('the church's own record supplies his documentation', 'its unpaid auditor'), the turn to the trial where 'power killed truth, and was wrong' is a genuine theological hinge, and the writer is in the dock first ('I have done my own version, repeated the damning anecdote about the other side without checking it'). Lyotard 1979, the 2016 Oxford word, John 18:38, Zechariah 8:16 and Ephesians 4:25 all check. The failure is slogan density: the first two paragraphs alone stack 'Not two interpretations. Two sets of facts.', 'truth changed employers', 'Facts have become uniforms. You do not examine a uniform.', and the essay keeps minting them ('Cynicism is not resistance to propaganda. It is propaganda's finished product.', 'wanting is the cheapest verification there is', 'Truth told at your own tribe's expense carries its verification inside it'), which is several attempted slogans where the standard asks for one earned verdict. About nine 'Not X. Y.' constructions in 2,469 words, and 'The instrument reads the same on both wrists' is the same right-left mirror template as the Leviticus essay. Also cite Arendt: the paraphrase is faithful to 'Truth and Politics' but a reader has nothing to check. Cut the aphorisms to two, keep the atheism and five-sons paragraph and the Pilate close, which are the essay's weight.

signals.thesis: Post-truth is Pilate's shrug democratized, the church has no standing to lecture on relativism until it obeys the ninth commandment against its own tribe, and truth told at one's own side's expense is the one argument that cannot be counterfeited.
stockPhrases: Say what is right in this before saying anything against it, because a great deal of it is right.
But watch what happens when the audit is asked to become a home.
Now notice the direction the temptation runs.
That is the entire test.
The instrument reads the same on both wrists.
unverifiable: Arendt paraphrase ('the slow destruction of the faculty that distinguishes true from false') names no work; it is consistent with 'Truth and Politics' (1967) and her 1974 interview, but as written the reader cannot check it

essay:affirmation-is-not-love.title: Is Affirmation the Same as Love?
essay:affirmation-is-not-love.notes: The thinking is sound and the mirror turns inward with unusual honesty ('I am fluent in warmth. I use it to license my silence.', 'I would rather be thanked than resented'), and the cruel-literalist counterfeit on the writer's own side is named before the close. Rieff 1966, Taylor 1991/2007, the 1986 California task force and Baumeister 2003 all check. Two failures. First, the register: about fourteen 'Not X. Y.' constructions ('The gospel does not affirm the self. It loves the self enough to tell it the truth.', 'It has become more afraid, and learned to call the fear kindness.'), four bolded slogan sentences ('Affirmation meets you in the tomb and brings flowers. Love meets you in the tomb and calls you out of it.'), a four-fragment paragraph ('Both tore truth and love apart. They were one thing in Jesus. They are meant to be one thing in us.'), and an anaphoric run ('Not while we were already fine. Not while we were being true to ourselves.'). Second, Scripture handling: quotations are italicized without references and drift across translations, Proverbs 27:6 in KJV wording, Romans 5:8 in NIV, 'Lazarus, come forth' in KJV, Proverbs 14:12 and Mark 10:21 unreferenced, and the Lewis line is a paraphrase inside quotation marks. Fix the references and translation first, then thin the verdicts and drop the bolding.

signals.thesis: Affirmation wills the comfort of the moment while love wills the good of the other; the church imported the therapeutic swap as grace and must recover a love that, like Christ at Lazarus's tomb, feels the loss and still calls the person out of it.
stockPhrases: So let me say plainly what this essay exists to argue.
Start by being fair to the thing, because the version worth refuting is the strong one
That is the swap. It happened so gently no one signed the papers.
Look at how Jesus loved, because he is the standard and our instincts are not.
I have to turn this on the church I am half-defending
until the bill comes due
unverifiable: Lewis quotation 'Love, having become a god, becomes a demon.' is not verbatim; The Four Loves gives it as 'begins to be a demon the moment he begins to be a god' (Lewis restating de Rougemont). Quote exactly or mark as paraphrase.
Proverbs 27:6 as quoted ('but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful') is KJV/NKJV, not ESV ('profuse are the kisses of an enemy'); no translation named.
Romans 5:8 as quoted ('God demonstrates his own love for us in this') is NIV, not ESV; no translation named.
Proverbs 14:12, Mark 10:21 ('Jesus looked at him and loved him'), and John 11:43 ('Lazarus, come forth', KJV) are quoted in italics with no reference traveling with the quote.

essay:authority-we-traded-for-authentici.title: Is the Bible the Final Word, or Am I?
essay:authority-we-traded-for-authentici.notes: The argument is real and the sources are the right ones used for their ideas rather than their names: Taylor's age of authenticity, Rieff's psychological man, Bellah's Sheila, MacIntyre's emotivism, Newbigin's public truth, the Bereans and Judges 21:25. The distinction between reading the text in its world and submitting the text to a prior verdict ('One submits to the passage to hear it more truly. The other submits the passage to a verdict reached before the page was open.') is the kind of named distinction the standard asks for. But the prose is the old register end to end: roughly thirty 'Not X. Y.' constructions in 3,195 words, one every hundred words ('Context is not the enemy. It is repentance.', 'That is not a feeling. It is a logical floor.', 'We did not lose the argument. We dismantled the court.', 'A god who only ever agrees with me is not a god. He is a mirror'), five bolded slogans, and two staged one-line fragment drops ('We thought we were gaining freedom. / We were changing kings.' and 'Authority was never the cage. / It was the hand reaching in.') that are the artificially dramatic hook the standard names by name. The ending accumulates verdicts and closes on manufactured intensity ('And I had been on my knees the whole time, in the dark, to me.'). This cannot be thinned by deletion because the sentences are built from the tic; keep the thesis, the context distinction, the Bereans, the pastoral paragraph about people whose floor opened, and rebuild the rest as paragraphs. 'At nineteen' is a specific biographical event not in the known facts and needs James's word, and the Sheila quotation is elided without marking.

signals.thesis: The progressive church did not abandon biblical authority but moved the throne from a word outside the self to lived experience inside it, and a faith ruled by the self can never confront the self; the right made the same trade in a louder voice.
stockPhrases: Say the claim plainly first, then spend the essay earning it.
Start by being fair to it, because the version worth refuting is the strong one.
Watch closely, because it never announces itself.
Now the hinge, set down without decoration.
Here is a test I have learned to run on myself, and it is merciless.
I have to turn now and aim this at my own side of the room
We thought we were gaining freedom. / We were changing kings.
Authority was never the cage. / It was the hand reaching in.
unverifiable: 'I made this trade myself, at nineteen, with both hands and gladly' and 'I traded it once myself, at nineteen' state a specific biographical event not among the known facts (atheism, raised without a father, five sons); confirm with James or remove the age.
Sheila Larson quotation is presented as continuous ('I believe in God. It's Sheilaism. Just my own little voice.') but Habits of the Heart has intervening sentences; mark the elision.

essay:cheap-grace-left-hand.title: When Forgiveness Only Flows One Way
essay:cheap-grace-left-hand.notes: Fairness is the essay's strength: it grants the conservative cheap grace first ('the progressive Christian who aims them there is not wrong'), restores Bonhoeffer to 'the room he was actually standing in' with the Deutsche Christen and Barmen 1934 correctly drawn and the honest note that he 'was not himself a signatory', and honors the left's fear that forgiveness 'has been said to abused women and exploited workers' before answering it. Volf 1996 and the Moltmann question, Niebuhr's Detroit years and 1932, Flossenbürg on April 9, 1945 all check; self-implication is specific ('I have throttled men over pennies while carrying a forgiven fortune'). The register is the old one: about fifteen 'Not X. Y.' constructions ('The test of grace was never the ally. It was always the enemy.', 'Not: if you have something against him. If he has something against you.', 'Not the sinner. The righteous one.'), five bolded slogans, and template section-openers ('Grant the obvious first', 'Hold that, and the left's version comes into focus', 'Watch the second move', 'So set the demand down without decoration', which is the same sentence the authority essay uses). Loose Scripture in three places (an unreferenced liturgical Matthew 6:12, a Luke/Matthew blend on tax collectors, Psalm 58:6 paraphrased). Keep the elder-brother movement and the closing image; rebuild the first three sections into developed paragraphs and drop the bolding.

signals.thesis: Bonhoeffer's cheap grace has a left-hand form, boundless mercy for allies and frozen wrath for enemies and absolution by alignment with the right cause, and costly grace means forgiving the actual enemy across the table.
stockPhrases: The claim, before any of the evidence.
Grant the obvious first, because the strong version of an argument is the only one worth making.
Hold that, and the left's version comes into focus.
Watch the second move, because it is subtler, and it is mine.
So set the demand down without decoration.
Here is the part that should stop every progressive Christian, and me first.
Be fair to the fear underneath the left's version
unverifiable: 'Forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors' is the liturgical/KJV-shaped form with no reference; Matthew 6:12 ESV reads 'as we also have forgiven our debtors'.
'even sinners manage that, even the tax collectors' blends Luke 6:32 (sinners) with Matthew 5:46 (tax collectors) under a Luke 6:27-28 citation.
'break their teeth, O God' is Psalm 58:6 quoted loosely (ESV: 'O God, break the teeth in their mouths') with no reference.

essay:conscience-outsourced-to-party.title: Should a Christian Follow a Political Party?
essay:conscience-outsourced-to-party.notes: The argument does accumulate (Haidt's groupishness, Bellah's civil religion, the Deutsche Christen and Barmen, then the Moral Majority as the right's mirror), and the Daniel window is a controlling image held long enough to work; the self-implication at "I have closed my own window and prayed toward the consensus" is concrete. But the gait is the old register: roughly twenty "Not X. Y." turns ("Not whether your politics are right. Whether they are yours." / "Agreement is not witness. Agreement is the sound a mirror makes." / "Not God in addition to men. Not God once we have checked with the coalition.") and six bolded slogan-verdicts where the standard asks for one earned thesis line. The claim that "the left's version is more dangerous precisely because the left believes it is the side that thinks for itself" is asserted, never argued, and it is exactly the asymmetric charge the voice standard says must be supported or dropped. The cut-flower paragraph ("a conviction cut from its root keeps its color for a while, the way a cut flower does") appears nearly verbatim in right-side-of-history, and the Newbigin "forty years to India... a Britain that had quietly stopped believing" sentence is shared with three other essays in this batch; a reader who opens two essays hears the same paragraph twice. Note also that here "my own tribe's mirror image" is the right (so the writer is placing himself on the left), while six-verses-we-memorized opens "I am a conservative-leaning pastor"; the self-implication is real in each essay but the tribal identity shifts to fit the target, which reads as manufactured biography across the corpus.

signals.thesis: Handing your conscience to a political tribe, left or right, is a capture that feels identical to conviction from the inside, and a conscience outsourced on small things will not be there when your own side asks you to call evil good.
stockPhrases: Watch how the fusion happens, because it never announces itself
The precision matters here, because precision is where the mercy hides
Hear that plainly
So how do you tell whether you have a conscience or a subscription?
unverifiable: "the left's version is more dangerous" (asserted without evidence; asymmetric responsibility claim)
Newbigin "gave forty years to India" (roughly 1936–1974, closer to 38; rounding, but repeated across four essays)
"Barth would have recognized the right's version on sight" (speculation presented as historical judgment)

essay:deconstruction-without-reconstruct.title: What Happens After You Deconstruct Your Faith?
essay:deconstruction-without-reconstruct.notes: This is the strongest architecture in the batch: it concedes the deconstructors' case first ("The people deconstructing their faith are usually right about why"), recovers Derrida's actual meaning, brings Polanyi, MacIntyre, and Taylor in where they explain the mechanism, then moves canonically through Matthew 12, Jeremiah 29, Nehemiah 4, Mark 9, Thomas, and Augustine, and the biography ("At nineteen I built an atheism brick by brick," "the weight of my father's absence") is consistent with the known facts and does real work. The ending ("a hammer was never a shelter and was never meant to be one") passes through the cross and empty tomb two paragraphs earlier and is the best-earned close of the eight. What keeps it from shipping as it stands: "Read the record: the ones who would not reconstruct assimilated into Babylon and dissolved, and history does not even keep their names" is an inference dressed as a historical record, the very thing the standard names as "vague claims presented as history"; the exile date conflates Jeremiah 29 (written to the 597 deportees) with 587; "the wave that crested around 2015... on TikTok" is anachronistic since the exvangelical hashtag dates to 2016 and TikTok's reach later; and both Scripture quotes drop the ESV exclamation ("I believe; help my unbelief!" / "My Lord and my God!") while presented as verbatim. About fourteen "Not X. Y." turns and four bolded verdicts ("**Especially to yourself.**") remain above the mature-register ceiling, and every section opens with the same one-sentence hook paragraph, a template shared with all eight essays. The Taylor immanent-frame and Newbigin paragraphs are near-verbatim duplicates of passages in right-side-of-history, when-justice-becomes-a-gospel, and conscience-outsourced-to-party.

signals.thesis: Deconstruction can be a faithful act, but deconstruction that never rebuilds is demolition, and the swept house is always re-occupied by an unexamined orthodoxy; the faithful model is doubt walked all the way to the wounds and built on again.
stockPhrases: Start with the word, because we have forgotten what it was for
Here is what I have watched, pastorally, across fifteen years
I want to be careful, because
The claim underneath the whole essay.

essay:right-side-of-history.title: When History Becomes Your God
essay:right-side-of-history.notes: The steelman is genuine and specific (Parker's 1853 sermon, King, Hegel's 1807 Phenomenology as the groundwater), Buck v. Bell with Holmes's verbatim line is exactly the kind of concrete, costly history the standard wants, and the Amos–Augustine–resurrection sequence is a real theological turn. But the essay is built from the old gait: eleven one- or two-sentence paragraphs in a 2,400-word piece ("We kept the arc. We threw away the hand that bends it." / "It is heaven for people who have stopped believing in heaven."), six bolded slogans, roughly sixteen antitheses, and a close that stacks three separate verdict-paragraphs ("There is one side worth being on. It was never the side of history." then "History is going to die.") where the standard asks for one. "Nostalgia and progressivism are the same idolatry facing opposite directions" is asserted in a single paragraph as symmetry the essay has not earned, and the whole "capture" paragraph ("biblically and gloriously right... a conviction cut from its root keeps its color") is copied from conscience-outsourced-to-party while the Augustine-in-410 paragraph and the "Here is the test... brutal, and I have failed it" opener are shared word-for-word with nostalgia-is-not-the-kingdom. King "carried that sentence into Birmingham" is loose; the arc line does not appear in the Birmingham letter, and he used it elsewhere. Self-implication is concrete ("I have caught myself weighing a sermon... by whether it would age well"), but the writer again places himself among progressives ("written to the people I agree with"), which contradicts the conservative self-placement elsewhere in this batch.

signals.thesis: "The right side of history" is a complete secular theology with its own god, salvation, and final judgment, adopted by the church without deciding to; the Christian future is judgment and mercy through a resurrection no trend predicted, not an arc that bends itself.
stockPhrases: Here is the question that breaks it, and there is no good answer

Watch how the capture actually happens, because it never announces itself

"the most quoted line in American moral life" (hyperbole stated as fact)
N. T. Wright "has spent a career arguing" (vague attribution; the idea is Wright's but no text is named)

essay:the-sin-we-stopped-naming.title: Why the Church Stopped Talking About Sin
essay:the-sin-we-stopped-naming.notes: The nearest thing to a pass in this batch, and the revise is surgical. It steelmans its own side before turning ("A generation reacted, and the reaction was right"), the H. Richard Niebuhr sentence is real and verbatim, Reinhold Niebuhr, Menninger, and Plantinga's "culpable shalom-breaking" each advance the diagnosis rather than decorate it, it names the other ditch ("the gospel with its arms cut off"), and the self-implication is the best in the set because it turns on the essay itself: "The temptation in writing an essay called The Sin We Stopped Naming is to name it in everyone but the author... There is no exit from this hall of mirrors that does not run through the first person." The ending ("the doctrine of sin, in the end, names the one naming it, and waits") passes through repentance and carries weight. Two things need confirming before it ships: "Niebuhr would later call original sin the one Christian doctrine empirically verifiable by a glance at the morning paper" is a widely repeated attribution whose exact source is contested and the "morning paper" gloss is the writer's embellishment, and "The publican said five words" is true only in the Greek (the ESV is seven) without saying so. Roughly eighteen antitheses is still heavy, though more of them are genuine hinges here ("His sin was not in his analysis. It was in his pronoun.") than in the other essays; "Good feelings have always been the cheapest disguise sin puts on" is lifted verbatim from right-side-of-history and "Once you see the trade, you cannot unsee it" is that essay's sentence with one word changed.

signals.thesis: Progressive Christianity recovered structural sin and lost personal sin, and the recovered half cut loose from the lost half has become the most respectable self-righteousness in the modern church; the Pharisee did not vanish, he changed parties.
stockPhrases: Read it slowly.
Here is the mechanism, and I am describing my own heart, not a stranger's
Now hear the other ditch, because it is real
This is the place to be exact

"The publican said five words" (five in Greek, seven in ESV; unexplained)
Matthew 4:17 rendered "repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near" (ESV reads "is at hand"; italicized as quotation)

essay:when-justice-becomes-a-gospel.title: When Justice Becomes a Gospel
essay:when-justice-becomes-a-gospel.notes: The concession at the top is real ("It is the gospel's own freight... When historians weigh us they will not be kind, and they should not be"), Rauschenbusch is handled fairly and specifically (Hell's Kitchen, 1917), and the Keller threat test with "I had built a calf, and it was beautiful, and it was made of everything I most admired" is honest self-implication. But the machine test fails on structure: the four-part gospel schema ("A fall... An election... An atonement... An end") and the four-paragraph anaphora "It cannot forgive. It cannot rest. It cannot extend grace to the dead... a fourth thing it cannot do" are perfect symmetry, a listicle wearing prose, and "eschatology for people who have stopped believing in eschatology" is right-side-of-history's "heaven for people who have stopped believing in heaven" recycled alongside the same Taylor fish-in-water paragraph. The essay also runs the same Luke 18 Pharisee, the same Niebuhr, and the same "I have prayed like the wrong man" beat as the-sin-we-stopped-naming, so the two pieces are largely one essay published twice. "Never me, always them, always the ones outside the circle of the awake" is partisan shorthand the standard forbids, and the right's counterpart idol gets one sentence and an unargued "it is worse" before "Both rooms are bowing" imposes symmetry. The ending re-runs the Pharisee parable and the Keller test it already stated, then lands on the reveal "In the mirror.", a device rather than earned weight.

signals.thesis: Justice that begins as the gospel's fruit can grow a rival gospel with its own fall, villain, salvation, and elect, and what it loses in the growing is grace for the people it has named the enemy; the way back is justice downstream of the cross, not upstream of it.
stockPhrases: Start where the conviction is strongest, because the version worth examining is the strong one
Hold that. All of it is true, and I am not walking any of it back.
Watch the substitution, because it is quiet
You can tell a counterfeit gospel by what it cannot do
the ones outside the circle of the awake
In the mirror.

Luke 18:9 quoted as "confident of their own righteousness who looked down on everyone else" (NIV wording, not ESV, presented in italics)
"that is the right's idol, and it is worse" (asymmetric claim asserted without argument)

essay:nostalgia-is-not-the-kingdom.title: Was America Ever Really a Christian Nation?
essay:nostalgia-is-not-the-kingdom.notes: The fairness is real ("The decline he feels is real. The numbers are real"), "Christian for whom" is the distinction that changes the argument, and Noll and Holland are used as witnesses whose ideas advance the diagnosis; "I have made that sound" and "I have let the gospel be my nation's chaplain" put the writer inside it concretely. The factual failure that must be fixed: "Three days out of Egypt, three days past the sea splitting open" attached to the pots-of-meat complaint conflates Exodus 15:22 (Marah, three days) with Exodus 16:3, which is a month into the wilderness. Structurally the essay is right-side-of-history turned around and it borrows that essay's prose to do it: the Augustine paragraph ("answered him with twenty-two books... the longest refusal in Christian literature") is near-verbatim, so are "The claim of this essay is blunt, and the rest of it is me earning the claim," "Here is the test, and it is brutal, and I have failed it," "Nostalgia and progressivism are the same idolatry," and the closing "the One who walked out of his own grave." Sixteen antitheses ("The golden age was not lost. It was a thing we agreed not to look at too closely.") and three bolded verdicts keep it in the old gait, and the coda "He has gone on ahead. He always does." softens an otherwise earned ending into a warm two-line tag.

signals.thesis: Nostalgia for a Christian America is idolatry, the mirror image of the progressive's worship of the future, because the golden age was iron for the people it excluded and the kingdom of God is always ahead of his people, never behind them.
stockPhrases: The claim of this essay is blunt, and the rest of it is me earning the claim
Here is where it stops being history and starts being the Bible
Read that slowly, because it is more severe than it sounds
Here is the test, and it is brutal, and I have failed it
He has gone on ahead. He always does.

Ecclesiastes 7:10 and Exodus 16:3 quoted in italics with wording that departs from ESV ("Do not say" / "pots of meat")
"a President who told the nation that faith was the bedrock of freedom" (unnamed, unsourced)
"the first Christian nationalist" applied to the Christian who wept for Rome (rhetorical, not historical)

essay:six-verses-we-memorized.title: Why Do Christians Quote Some Verses and Skip Others?
essay:six-verses-we-memorized.notes: This is the fairest essay in the batch on its own terms: it gives Romans 13 and the order texts their honest case ("order is a gift, that anarchy is not holiness"), reads Romans 13 to verse 8, quotes Leviticus 19:33–34 and Amos 5 accurately, names the left's own skipped list without forcing equivalence, and the shelf confession ("I have given Romans 13 its full Sunday. I am not sure I have ever given Leviticus 19:34 a single one") is the most concrete self-implication of the eight. It cannot ship because of the numbers: "the God who wrote all eighty thousand of them" is simply wrong (the Bible has roughly 31,100 verses), "the roughly two thousand verses about money and the poor that scholars have been tallying for decades" is the contested Wallis/Sider tally presented as settled scholarship with no scholar named, and "the other sixty" is a rhetorical figure built for the six/sixty symmetry that the essay then treats as a count ("could not, on its best day, produce three of them"). Paragraphs are developed and fragments are few, which is the mature register, but thirteen antitheses ("You have not honored the text. You have quarried it.") and the template opener "So here is the test, and I have failed it" remain. The ending is earned from Matthew 25 but stops at judgment ("he is going to ask, on a day none of us schedules") with no pass through mercy for the church it has just indicted, which the standard asks for when the subject warrants it.

signals.thesis: A tribe edits the Bible by emphasis rather than deletion, and the American right has built a working canon out of a dozen texts like Romans 13:1 while filing the commands on the stranger and the poor under "context," because those verses cost something the memorized ones do not.
stockPhrases: Start by being fair, because
Here is the trouble with a memorized verse
Here is the turn, and it does not let the other side off either
So here is the test, and I have failed it
unverifiable: "the God who wrote all eighty thousand of them" (factually wrong; ~31,100 verses)
"the roughly two thousand verses about money and the poor that scholars have been tallying for decades" (contested popular tally; no scholar named)
"the other sixty" verses (a rhetorical number treated as a count)
Matthew 25 "the word translated stranger is the word for foreigner, the immigrant" (xenos means stranger/foreigner; "immigrant" is a stretch)

essay:strongman-theology.title: Why a Frightened Church Wants a King
essay:strongman-theology.notes: This one ships. It stays inside its controlling text long enough for the text to do the work (the six "he will take"s of 1 Samuel 8:11–17 are counted correctly), Brueggemann's royal consciousness and Niebuhr's 1932 argument explain the mechanism rather than decorate it, and the Bonhoeffer radio address of 1 February 1933 is dated and described accurately. The steelman is the best in the batch and it is where the mature register shows: "And the fear is not always irrational. This is the part I refuse to wave away... They are not imagining the threat. The threat has a return address." The paragraphs are full, only three one-sentence paragraphs in 2,500 words, and the repetitions ("and the Lord did not answer in that day") are measured and gain weight each time rather than becoming a tic; the antitheses here are mostly the essay's actual hinges ("The judgment was not the king. The judgment was getting the king."). The ending passes through the cross ("He fought the decisive battle of all history from a cross, unarmed, apparently losing") and lands on one earned line. Two things to note without holding the piece: the italicized 1 Samuel 8:11–18 passage is a condensed splice of the verses in order rather than a continuous quotation and would read more honestly as paraphrase, and the bolded "Fear hears 'he will fight your battles' and never finishes the sentence" restates the plain sentence just before it. Self-implication runs on "we" more than "I" ("the church I belong to is the church praying the prayer"), thinner than elsewhere but honestly placed.

signals.thesis: A frightened people does not ask for a tyrant but for a protector, and the protector becomes what it feared once the fear has been handed to him; 1 Samuel 8 is the mirror for a church reaching for a strongman.
stockPhrases: Here is the engine under all of it, and it is not politics
Read the verb.
Read the logic.
And here is the verdict I cannot soften
unverifiable: 1 Samuel 8:11–18 presented in italics as a single quotation but condensed from several verses (words and order accurate; omissions unmarked)
Bonhoeffer's broadcast "was cut off the air before he finished" (traditional account; whether it was censorship or a time cut is debated, and the essay does not claim censorship)

essay:the-flag-in-the-sanctuary.title: Why Is There a Flag in the Sanctuary?
essay:the-flag-in-the-sanctuary.notes: The argument genuinely accumulates (military funeral steelman, 312/313, Bellah 1967, Bellamy 1892, 1954/1956/1957, Exodus 20, Daniel 3, Matthew 22, Augustine) and the dates check out, but the gait is old-register: roughly twelve 'Not X. Y.' hinges ('These were not acts of revival. They were acts of statecraft'; 'That is not honor. That is the golden image with better music'; 'An idol is rarely a demon. It is usually a blessing promoted past its station'), so the tic outnumbers the hinge. The piece signposts its own architecture ('Let me be fair before I am sharp', 'Now the theological turn, and it is sharper than the history') and closes on a one-line question, 'Whose image are you.', which leaves the accused exposed rather than opening toward repentance. Self-implication is declared ('the people I am describing are my people', 'I have stood in that room') but never shown; the 'we' who 'sang the national anthem over the swap' never becomes an 'I' who did. Exodus 20:4 is quoted as 'an idol' (ESV reads 'carved image') with no translation named.

signals.thesis: The flag in the sanctuary is the visible seam of the Constantinian fusion of cross and nation; civil religion is a counterfeit that works because it is close enough to pass, and the coin question forces the reader to decide whose image he bears.
stockPhrases: Let me be fair before I am sharp
Start with what is true in it, because the version worth challenging is the sincere one
Now the theological turn, and it is sharper than the history
And here is where the American chapter turns specific
Once you can see the seam, you cannot stop seeing it
Whose image are you.

essay:the-persecution-we-invented.title: Is the American Church Really Being Persecuted?
essay:the-persecution-we-invented.notes: The self-implication is the strongest in the batch and concrete ('I preach to people who reach for this word and I have not always corrected them gently'; 'I have used the word loosely myself'), and the Taylor/Holland/Stark/Newbigin witnesses each advance the diagnosis rather than decorate it. But the essay is sharp before it is fair: the opening paragraph sneers ('Several of them got book deals') on the strength of unattributed anecdotes ('a famous pastor calls it the catacombs', 'the word from the conference stage is martyrdom') and only then says 'So I want to be careful here.' Antithesis is the default gait, thirteen by my count with 'That is not X. That is Y.' five times ('That is not analysis. That is theater'; 'That is not solidarity. That is theft'; 'That is not a catastrophe. That is an opportunity'). One sentence is garbled ('the strong owe the strong nothing'), 'Tom Holland, the historian, not the actor' is a joke the register does not want, and 'It is Tuesday' reads as brand insertion. The ending passes through the cross and is earned.

signals.thesis: The most powerful religious body in history has taught itself to feel hunted; the New Testament word belongs to people actually dying, and misusing it costs the American church the freedom that losing its throne could have given it.
stockPhrases: Sit with what that means
Here is what makes our use of the word

Walk it forward, because the cost is not abstract
So here is where it leaves me
Start with what is true, because the version of this argument worth making is the fair one
It is Tuesday.
Tom Holland, the historian, not the actor
