John 15:18 rendered 'it hated me before it hated you' — ESV reads 'it has hated me before it hated you'

essay:the-third-temptation.title: Why Did Jesus Refuse the Offer of Political Power?
essay:the-third-temptation.notes: The exegetical spine is strong (Matthew 4 against John 6:15, Philippians 2 'grasped', Mark 10:42–45) and the confession is real ('Here is the test, and it is brutal, and I have failed it'; 'I have wanted the mountain'). What the essay never does is draw the distinction the mature register prizes between ordinary civic participation and idolatrous grasping; 'the prospect of a court reshaped, a law passed, an election won' is treated as the tempter's offer wholesale, which a Christian who voted to end a real injustice would not sign. The antithesis count is around fifteen ('He is not describing a different way to use power. He is describing a different thing altogether'; 'It does not feel like the third temptation. It feels like faithfulness'), plus a 'precisely how... precisely how... precisely how' anaphora, and the close is a fragment stack ('We have not been giving it. That is not the world's failure. It is ours.') that leaves the church exposed with no way home. 'Here is the test, and it is brutal' recurs verbatim in the precinct essay, a machine tell. Matthew 4:9 is italicized twice as 'All this I will give you' where ESV reads 'All these', and the Grand Inquisitor's lines are italicized as if verbatim when they are translation-dependent paraphrase.

signals.thesis: The third temptation, the kingdoms in exchange for worship, is the one the church keeps failing; a church that grasps political power to advance the kingdom has accepted the offer Jesus refused on the tempter's own terms.
stockPhrases: Be fair to the temptation, because the version worth refusing is the strong one
That is the genius of it.
Here is the test, and it is brutal, and I have failed it.
Now the place where the New Testament settles it
Read it against the temptation and the symmetry is exact
precisely how... and precisely how... and precisely how
Not money. Not pleasure. Not even survival.
unverifiable: Matthew 4:9 italicized as 'All this I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me' — ESV reads 'All these'
Luke 4:6 'I give it to whomever I will' — ESV reads 'to whom I will'
Grand Inquisitor lines italicized as quotation ('We have corrected your work', 'We are not with you. We are with him') are paraphrase of a translation, not verbatim
'Bonhoeffer named it for what it was: not a tactical error but apostasy' — judgment attributed without a source

essay:two-kingdoms-one-pledge.title: Can You Pledge Allegiance to Two Kingdoms?
essay:two-kingdoms-one-pledge.notes: The flattery paragraph is the best distinction in the batch ('A church that is hunted knows it has a second country... A church that is honored can go a hundred years without ever discovering it has a second country at all'), the abuse of the doctrine is conceded honestly, and Augustine and Luther 1523 are used as witnesses that do work. But there is a factual error that must come out: 'Bonhoeffer helped write the Barmen Declaration of 1934' is false (Barth drafted it; Bonhoeffer was in London), and the radio address was two days after January 30, not 'weeks after'. Matthew 6:24 is quoted in NIV wording without naming the translation. The thesis leans on an etymology ('a feudal word, the oath a vassal swore') and on an assertion ('a posture our ancestors would have recognized instantly as the posture of worship') its opponents would not grant. Fifteen antitheses ('It is not a doctrine of withdrawal. It is a doctrine of ordered love'; 'Not we would prefer to. Not in extreme cases. Must.') and a closing image ('The music will play again, and the room will stand') that duplicates the flag essay's ending almost move for move. Self-implication is asserted ('I am inside this, not above it') but never given a concrete instance.

signals.thesis: Allegiance is singular by nature; the Christian swore it to a crucified King before any nation asked, so a national pledge can be a love but never an allegiance, and the two-kingdoms tradition exists to keep that order.
stockPhrases: That is the whole essay, so let me say it plainly
So let me be fair to the country before I am honest about the cost
Begin with the strongest form of the loyalty I am about to question, because the weak form is not worth refuting
So here is the cost, stated as plainly as I can state it
Jesus settled the arithmetic of allegiance
The music will play again, and the room will stand
Not we would prefer to. Not in extreme cases. Must.
unverifiable: 'Bonhoeffer helped write the Barmen Declaration of 1934' — incorrect; Barmen was drafted principally by Karl Barth with Asmussen and Breit, and Bonhoeffer was in London
'In 1933, weeks after Hitler took power, he gave a radio address' — the Führer/Verführer address was February 1, 1933, two days after January 30
Matthew 6:24 quoted as 'Either you will hate the one and love the other... You cannot serve both God and money' — NIV wording, translation unnamed
'in a posture our ancestors would have recognized instantly as the posture of worship' — asserted without support

essay:when-the-pulpit-became-a-precinct.title: When Your Church Became a Voting Bloc
essay:when-the-pulpit-became-a-precinct.notes: This is the best-argued of the political five: the steelman is real ('There is no villain in it... a series of sensible men solving real problems with the tool that happened to be working'), the woman three pews back keeps the victim visible, Hunter's ressentiment and John 17:21 do actual diagnostic work, and the pastor's confession is concrete ('where you let the tribe's enemies stand in for sin so you never have to name the sin in the room'). It still fails the mature register on gait: eighteen 'Not X. Y.' constructions by my count, the heaviest of the political set ('The capture does not require corruption. It only requires...'; 'Not a personality difference. Not a healthy diversity of emphasis. A tearing of the one body'; 'We did not just divide the body. We falsified the evidence'), so the hinge has become the default sentence. 'Here is the test for any church, and it is brutal' is the same sentence the third-temptation essay uses, and every captured church described here votes one direction, which the essay should either own or widen. The ending is earned and concrete (the coat, the door), but there is no way home after the diagnosis; 'The will to power, Hunter wrote, leaves a residue' reads as a quotation without being one.

signals.thesis: A church is captured not when it endorses a candidate but when belonging to the tribe and belonging to Christ become the same feeling, a capture that happens through reasonable steps and costs the church its witness and the people it quietly drove out.
stockPhrases: Be fair to how it happened, because nobody walked into apostasy on purpose
Here is the test for any church, and it is brutal, and most of ours would fail it
Walk the room the capture builds and count who is missing
Now stand outside the church and look back at it, because this is where the real cost lands
this is the cost nobody puts on the books
Not a personality difference. Not a healthy diversity of emphasis.
unverifiable: 'The will to power, Hunter wrote, leaves a residue' — presented as near-quotation; wording unverified against To Change the World (the ressentiment argument itself is real)
John 17:21 condensed to 'that they may all be one, so that the world may believe' without marking the elision

essay:proof-texting.title: How Both Sides Use the Bible to Win
essay:proof-texting.notes: Closest to a pass in the batch. The paragraphs are developed, the coin and the stone-in-the-wall images are sustained rather than swapped every paragraph, Job's friends and Satan's Psalm 91 are used as arguments rather than ornaments, and the discipline section ('Before you spend the coin, ask where it was minted') is the symptom-cause-wisdom movement done properly. Seven antitheses, several of them earned hinges ('He out-reads the devil. He does not out-quote him'). What keeps it from shipping: 2 Peter 3:16 is italicized as Scripture in non-ESV wording ('distort, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction'), which breaks the site's own verbatim rule; the writer never enters the indictment in first person, the proof-texter is 'he' throughout and 'the vice of all of us' is the only concession, when the 'Both tribes do it' section is exactly where a preacher should name his own canon within the canon; and the 'This is the trap / This is the lesson / That is the real cost' signposts repeat. The ending's last clause is earned, though the sentence before it restates the 'willingness to lose' paragraph.

signals.thesis: Proof-texting, treating verses as detachable units of authority, is how both sides claim Scripture, and its real cost is that the reader loses the ability to be addressed by the Word.
stockPhrases: This is the trap.
This is the lesson the church keeps refusing to learn.
That is the real cost.
Same words. Opposite comfort.
The convenient verse is the dangerous verse.
unverifiable: 2 Peter 3:16 italicized as 'distort, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction' — ESV reads 'twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures'; translation unnamed and order altered
N. T. Wright's drama 'in acts' listed as six (creation, fall, Israel, Jesus, church, new creation) — Wright's own scheme is five acts

essay:reading-in-community.title: Why Should You Read the Bible in Community?
essay:reading-in-community.notes: The thinking is sound and the guard against relativism is exactly the distinction the register asks for ('That would only be the consumer lens wearing a passport... Community is not relativism'); the steelman of the tribe ('right about almost everything and wrong about the one thing it cannot see') is honest, and Acts 15 is read as a council rather than a proof text. But the antithesis is the engine and the gait at once, around fifteen ('He calls this discernment. It is curation'; 'It can deepen you. It cannot turn you'; 'They did not take a poll... They did not let... They did not split'), and the writer never names his own tribe; the echo chamber section is all 'he' and 'the modern Christian', which is where a pastor who chose his teachers should have come in. Two attributions need checking: Andrew Walls's Ephesian moment is grounded in Ephesians 2 and 4:13, and the claim that he 'noticed the strange phrase: with all the saints' in 3:18 is unverified; Brueggemann is name-dropped for a sentence that says the same thing without him. Lewis wrote 'clean sea breeze of the centuries', not 'wind'. 'Every previous essay in this project' is series scaffolding a reader on the site cannot see.

signals.thesis: A tribe confirms you and a community corrects you; Scripture was given to a people across cultures and centuries so that readers unlike you can see the lens you cannot see yourself.
stockPhrases: The cruelest part of the trap is
There is a hard distinction to hold here, because the point can be abused
Notice what the council did not do, because the omissions are the lesson
a larger echo chamber with better production values
a tribe wearing a community's clothes
the consumer lens wearing a passport
unverifiable: Andrew Walls's 'Ephesian moment' attributed to his noticing 'with all the saints' in Ephesians 3:18 — Walls grounds it in Ephesians 2 (Jew and Gentile as one new humanity) and 4:13; the 3:18 linkage is unverified
Ephesians 3:18 quoted as 'power to comprehend' — ESV reads 'strength to comprehend'
'Walter Brueggemann read the Scriptures as a long conversation the people of God have been having for millennia' — uncited; the sentence stands without the name
C. S. Lewis 'the wind of the centuries blowing through the mind' — Lewis wrote 'the clean sea breeze of the centuries' (introduction to Athanasius, On the Incarnation)

essay:six-lenses-that-distort-the-bible.title: How Does Your Culture Shape the Way You Read the Bible?
essay:six-lenses-that-distort-the-bible.notes: Taylor's background, Smith's liturgies, and the 2 Corinthians 3–4 veil are used as real mechanism, the nationalism paragraph refuses the cheap symmetry ('America into the promised land and... into Babylon are wearing the same lens facing opposite directions'), and the Emmaus turn ('We do not argue our way out of our distortions. We are met our way out of them') earns the ending. But this is the heaviest old-register piece in the batch: twenty-six 'Not X. Y.' constructions by my count, nearly one per hundred words, so almost every paragraph closes on a snapped antithesis ('He thinks he is bringing a blank mind to the text. He is bringing a trained heart'; 'The biblical word for our condition is not bias. It is veil'; 'The goal is not glasslessness. The goal is...'), and the two-by-three symmetry of the lenses ('how the self got large' / 'how the cross got comfortable') is the perfect parallelism the standard names as sounding generated. Each lens is asserted rather than conceded first; only individualism gets a 'which is not nothing'. The writer never says which lens he wears, and Scripture arrives in unmarked non-ESV wording: Joshua 5:14 as 'Neither' (NIV; ESV 'No') and 1 Corinthians 13:12 in altered KJV. At this density the revision is near the rewrite border.

signals.thesis: You read the Bible through a lens your culture ground before you opened the book; six lenses (individualism, consumerism, nationalism, therapeutic, prosperity, partisanship) filter the text before interpretation begins, and only encounter with Christ, not sophistication, lifts the veil.
stockPhrases: Here is the difficulty that makes all of this hard
That detail is worth sitting in
should unsettle every confident reader
his turn is the one that should frighten us most
which is how you know it is load-bearing
Name the glass and it loses some of its power. So name it.
There is no view from nowhere.
unverifiable: Joshua 5:14 italicized as 'Neither.' — NIV wording; ESV reads 'No'; translation unnamed
1 Corinthians 13:12 quoted as 'Now we see through a glass, darkly; then we shall see face to face' — altered KJV, translation unnamed
'Richard Hays spent a career showing how even the New Testament writers read their own Scriptures through a lens' — uncited to a work

essay:the-whole-counsel.title: Why You Can't Cherry-Pick the Bible
essay:the-whole-counsel.notes: Developed paragraphs throughout, and the Wright/Emmaus material does real work, but antithesis is the gait rather than the hinge (13 by count: "The doctrine guards the gate. The avoidance empties the house"; "The whole counsel is not a quota of coverage. It is the only context..."), and the four-fold "grace cut off from holiness becoming license, holiness cut off from grace becoming cruelty, sovereignty cut off from love becoming fatalism, love cut off from judgment becoming sentiment" is the perfect symmetry the standard names as a machine tell. The indictment stays on "the man who edits by avoidance" and "he"; the writer never enters in the first person, and the "test you can run on yourself" paragraph is where a pastor of fifteen years should have named his own unopened books. Acts 20 is stretched: "warnings that made them angry" is not in the speech (20:31 has admonition with tears only). Four bold pull-quotes where the standard asks for one at a genuine hinge. The ending is earned ("We have withheld plenty, not from others, but from ourselves") and should survive the revision intact.

signals.thesis: Cherry-picking is the American hermeneutic, and because the verses you skip warp the verses you keep, only reading the whole canon in course lets Scripture correct rather than confirm you.
stockPhrases: Here is a test you can run on yourself, and it stings
This is the deep reason cherry-picking fails
That is the tell
This is why cherry-picking is not merely incomplete
unverifiable: Acts 20 speech glossed as including "warnings that made them angry" — not in the text; Acts 20:31 has only admonition with tears
Brueggemann's "structure-legitimating texts and the pain-embracing texts" — real Brueggemann vocabulary but attributed without a titled work
"Every serious distortion in Christian history has been a true emphasis grown cancerous by isolation" — sweeping historical claim asserted, not evidenced

essay:what-the-original-audience-heard.title: What the First Readers of the Bible Actually Heard
essay:what-the-original-audience-heard.notes: Nearest to a pass in the batch: it accumulates from Bailey through Walton to Jonah and Philemon, steelmans the honest fear ("has God hidden his word behind a wall of scholarship only experts can climb") and answers it without condescension ("The plain reader gets the house"), and the ending returns to the man on the hill outside Nineveh with real weight. What keeps it from shipping is the register: roughly 15 antitheses ("Jesus was not being friendly. He was redrawing the boundary"; "This is not trivia. It is the difference between a parable that comforts and a parable that detonates") and matched triplets ("We are the good Samaritan, never the lawyer. We are Jonah's God, never Jonah. We are Paul, never Philemon") that make the prose sound built rather than thought. The Philemon line given in quotation marks ("no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother") is not verbatim in ESV or any standard translation and should be offered as paraphrase. Three rhetorical questions are missing their question marks, which reads as a mechanical scrub. Self-implication is a genuine "we" throughout but never reaches "I."

signals.thesis: Scripture was written to people distant from us in culture, cosmos, and medium, and recovering what they heard restores both the scandal and, more costly, the indictment that modern readers have edited themselves out of.
stockPhrases: This is the gap I want to make visible
And here is the quiet tragedy of distant reading
There is a deeper layer still
There is a fear that has to be answered here
Consider what happens to the word "kingdom" alone
unverifiable: Philemon 16 quoted as "no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother" — ESV reads "no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother"; the quoted form matches no standard translation
N. T. Wright's exile/kingdom reading characterized with no work named
Nineveh described as "the capital of Assyria" for Jonah's audience — it became capital under Sennacherib, later than the book's setting; defensible for the book's readers, but stated flat

essay:christendom-is-ending.title: What the End of Christian America Actually Means
essay:christendom-is-ending.notes: The history is specific and correct (312, 380, Murray's list of shifts, Kreider, Taylor), the Constantinian settlement gets a fair hearing through Holland before its cost is named ("I want to be fair to it before I name its cost"), and the self-implication is concrete and first-person: "I have stood in my own pulpit and addressed an audience of the imagination." But it runs on one-sentence hook paragraphs as section openers ("But here is what the gift cost." "Take away the scaffolding and you find out what was load-bearing.") and roughly 17 antitheses, and it closes on the fragment triplet "The stone was never the statue. It was always the stone. And the stone outlasts the gold," the old register's verdict-stack bolted onto a paragraph that had already landed. "It was, in many ways, a gift" is the exact hedge the revision pass names. The "anxious voices" who want to "recapture the culture, seize the institutions" are dismissed ("it deserves to fail") without the steelman the essay extends to Constantine. The opening anecdote and the unattributed "see how they love one another" (Tertullian, Apology 39) need marking.

signals.thesis: What is ending is Christendom, the cultural default backed by state power, not Christianity; its death is the deferred cost of the Constantinian trade and returns the church to the conditions of its own beginning.
stockPhrases: But here is what the gift cost
Here is what I have come to believe the end requires
It is worth saying at the outset why this matters
There is a pattern worth naming here
in many ways, a gift
unverifiable: "A man I know turned seventy this year, and he can remember when the stores in his town closed on Sunday" — anecdote, not checkable
"see how they love one another" — Tertullian, Apology 39, presented as what pagans said without attribution
Christendom credited with "the very concept of human rights" — sweeping, stated beyond what Holland is cited for

essay:exile-is-not-the-end.title: How Should the Church Think About Losing Cultural Power?
essay:exile-is-not-the-end.notes: Jeremiah 29 is held long enough to do theological work, and the "What an exile actually does on a Tuesday" section is exactly the standard's ordinary-Tuesday move. But the writer never enters the indictment: "Most of our energy goes the other direction, toward demanding the allegiance and neglecting the welfare" is the paragraph where a working pastor should have said what he himself has demanded of his city, and the culture-warrior is sketched as "the symbolic victory that feels like resistance and accomplishes nothing" rather than given the strongest case his own defenders would sign. Around 17 antitheses ("Loss did not impoverish their faith. It forced their faith to become portable"; "Acceptance is not surrender"), an imperative stack ("So build the house. Plant the garden. Seek the welfare of the city..."), and a closing that restates the title as slogan ("The exile is long. It is not the end. It was never the end") after the previous paragraph had already ended it on "The center was never the point." "Sit with how strange that is" is a stock turn. "The synagogue... was an exile invention" and "the most durable religious legacy in human history" are stated flat where the first is disputed and the second is unfalsifiable.

signals.thesis: The Western church's loss of cultural standing is exile in the biblical sense, and Jeremiah 29 commands settling in and seeking the city's welfare rather than assimilation or separatism, because exile was Israel's most fertile period and is the church's normal condition.
stockPhrases: Sit with how strange that is
Here is the part the New Testament makes impossible to dodge
This is, I think, the most overlooked instruction
There is a strange freedom in accepting the exile
There is a discipline in this that the comfortable church never had to learn
unverifiable: "The synagogue... was an exile invention, born of necessity when the temple was gone" — the origin of the synagogue is genuinely disputed; stated as settled fact
"the most durable religious legacy in human history" — unfalsifiable superlative
"The Torah was edited and compiled by a people who had lost the land it described" — critical consensus presented flat under Brueggemann's name without qualification
Newbigin characterized with no work named

essay:the-numbers-behind-the-decline.title: Is the Church Really Dying? What the Numbers Say
essay:the-numbers-behind-the-decline.notes: The data handling is the most honest thing in the batch ("I give you a range on purpose"; "directional, not decimal"; the "closet emptying rather than a faith collapsing" point), and Burge, Putnam, and Taylor are used for what they actually argue. But it points outward the whole way: "the pastor who calls the data a lie," "the fearful church grasps, manipulates, and chases the culture," while the writer only "watched" the harm; there is no paragraph where he admits leading from fear himself, though the companion essay on discipling fear does exactly that. Roughly 20 antitheses ("The fear was not too few. The fear was too many"; "Sociology describes what has happened. It does not prophesy"), and the ending recaps the two camps from paragraph one ("do not be the pastor who calls the data a lie... do not be the pastor who reads it as the final verdict") before a fragment triplet and a bolded slogan. The 1 Kings 19:18 quotation is actually the Romans 11:4 wording, and Christian Smith's "moralistic therapeutic deism" needs its source (Soul Searching, 2005) and co-author Denton.

signals.thesis: The decline data are real but their meaning is contested; much of the rise of the "nones" is deflation of nominal affiliation and a collapse of belonging rather than belief, and Scripture never treated the headcount as the score.
stockPhrases: This is the first place the numbers lie when handled carelessly
This matters more than it first appears, because it changes the diagnosis
This is why I distrust the graph
and it deserves naming
It helps to understand why religion surveys are so slippery
unverifiable: 1 Kings 19:18 quoted as "I have kept for myself seven thousand who have not bowed to Baal" — that is Romans 11:4's wording; ESV 1 Kings 19:18 reads "Yet I will leave seven thousand in Israel, all the knees that have not bowed to Baal"
Christian Smith's "moralistic therapeutic deism" cited without the work (Soul Searching, 2005) or co-author Melinda Lundquist Denton
"The early church grew in part because it was conspicuously unafraid, unafraid of plague" — Stark's plague argument, unattributed here

essay:what-dies-when-christendom-dies.title: What Actually Dies When Christianity Loses Power
essay:what-dies-when-christendom-dies.notes: The pastoral posture is exactly right. "We do not get to be glad they are gone. We get to ask why the only Christianity many of them ever encountered was the cultural counterfeit" turns the indictment onto the church before the leavers, and the second list ("Real goods are dying too") refuses the cheap version of the argument; Bonhoeffer and Hebrews 12 are accurate and load-bearing. The failure is structural: the "What dies:" and "What does not die:" paragraphs are fragment inventories, and the husk/seed antiphon ("The reserved seat at the civic table, husk. The conviction that Jesus is Lord whether the civic table agrees or not, seed. The expectation of cultural deference, husk...") is six-fold perfect symmetry, the machine tell the standard names by name. About 15 antitheses, four bold lines, and essay-about-itself signposting ("That is the sober part of this essay, and I will not soften it"). "The pastors who had the most religion had the least faith" reads as Bonhoeffer's finding but is the essayist's gloss. The ending passes through John 12:24 and earns "Something is supposed to grow here."

signals.thesis: Cultural Christianity and the faith are dying in the same grave, and the church's work is to sort them: grieve the genuine goods Christendom carried, refuse to mourn the husk, and trust that the seed's death precedes a harvest.
stockPhrases: And here is the part the church struggles to say out loud
So let me say plainly what I think dies
That is the sober part of this essay, and I will not soften it
There is a second list worth making, harder than the first
This is the test that separates the two things dying in the same grave
unverifiable: "The pastors who had the most religion had the least faith" — placed inside the Bonhoeffer paragraph so it reads as his finding; it is the essayist's own sentence
"The faith was supposed to be finished when Rome fell" — unsourced; who expected this is never said
Bonhoeffer's 1944 letters cited generally — "religionless Christianity" and "come of age" are real, but no letter is dated

essay:witness-without-power.title: How Did the Early Church Grow Without Political Power?
essay:witness-without-power.notes: Best architecture in the batch: Stark and Kreider are used for their actual findings, 1 Corinthians 1 and 2 Corinthians 12 govern the diagnosis rather than decorate it, the opposing case is given its strongest form before it is answered ("The case for seizing power is not stupid... Law teaches... The defender's exhibit is abolition and the civil rights movement"), and the writer is inside the indictment in the first person ("I include myself and my own tribe in the failure"; "I am still, most days, learning to want it"). What blocks a pass is the gait: roughly 22 antitheses ("Not tolerated in weakness. Not despite weakness. Made perfect in it"; "A church that rules looks like every other ruler. A church that serves, forgives, and suffers looks like its Lord"), the built triplet "out-loved, out-suffered, and out-died," and four bold pull-quotes. Hauerwas's "first political task is to be the church" is his real thesis but no work is cited. The ending is earned: the plague bedside returns from the opening and "We just got rich enough, for a while, to forget it" implicates rather than consoles. Revision here is trimming, not rebuilding.

signals.thesis: The early church grew without power and in a sense because of it, through patient, costly, relational witness, and the Western church's loss of power returns it to the only method that ever worked.
stockPhrases: That is the fact a declining Western church most needs to sit with
There is a cost to this recovery that I do not want to soften
This matters because it cuts against everything
I want to name what this asks of pastors in particular
Notice that Paul had asked God three times
unverifiable: Hauerwas's "the church's first political task is not to seize the levers of the state but to be the church" — real Hauerwas/Willimon thesis (Resident Aliens, 1989) but no work named
"The early church had no pastors with public standing; it had elders who were as likely to be arrested as honored" — generalization, unsourced

essay:discipling-people-out-of-fear.title: How Fear Took Over the Church
essay:discipling-people-out-of-fear.notes: The most pastorally honest piece in the batch: the frightened man is given his real wounds before any correction ("afraid for his grandchildren... afraid in the specific, sleepless way of a person who has been told every night for years that the barbarians are at the gate"), the self-implication arrives in paragraph three ("I do not exempt myself... The pastor who imagines he is above the fear is usually just better at hiding it, including from himself") and gets its own section, every Scripture quotation checks verbatim against ESV, Smith's liturgical anthropology is used for what it actually says, and the ending passes through the cross ("held in hands that were nailed open, and they have not let go yet"). It still walks on antithesis, 24 by count, the highest here ("The politics is the surface. The fear is the engine"; "A man who knows he is afraid can be comforted. A man who believes his fear is simply accurate perception cannot"), and three sections open on the same "There is a [step / hard turn / turn] here" template. The Peterson attribution "proceeds at the pace of grace" I could not verify as his phrase; it must be sourced or cut before this ships. "Decapacitating" should be "incapacitating." The fear as pictured codes only one political direction; the mechanism is not partisan, and one sentence saying so would keep the guardrail from firing one way.

signals.thesis: Political capture in the church is a formation problem running on fear, not an information problem, so pastors must disciple the fear itself through the church's counter-liturgy, beginning with their own.
stockPhrases: This is the thing about political capture that we keep misdiagnosing
This is why argument fails
There is a step before the long formation
There is a hard turn here that I have to make on myself
There is a turn here that changes how a pastor feels
This is enormously freeing for the pastor
unverifiable: Eugene Peterson "called the pastoral vocation a work that proceeds at the pace of grace" — could not verify this as Peterson's phrase; source it or cut it
"the daily three hours of cable news" — unsourced consumption figure
Psalm 46:10 quoted verbatim but with the ESV exclamation point dropped ("I will be exalted in the earth!")

essay:pastoring-a-captured-congregation.title: How Do You Pastor a Church Addicted to Cable News?
essay:pastoring-a-captured-congregation.notes: This is the one in the batch that actually accumulates: it respects the rival before naming its lie ("we should respect a rival before we name its lie... It is, in the precise sense, a liturgy"), draws the load-bearing distinction ("name the capture itself, the condition, not the channel"), moves through Romans 14 and Ephesians 4 with the references traveling, and gives self-implication a whole section rather than a sentence ("the pastor who imagines himself dry is usually the one already soaked"; "whose funerals we are warm at and whose we are merely correct at"). Peterson's "shopkeepers" is really the opening of Working the Angles, Resident Aliens is correctly dated 1989, and every ESV quotation checks. The ending passes through the cross without an altar call ("where enemies eat as brothers because a third party has made peace between them at his own expense. We have not yet begun to use it"). The one thing I would touch: nine "Not X. Y." turns in 2,500 words is more than the argument needs, though most sit inside developed paragraphs and are doing real distinguishing work; loosening two or three ("This is not a metaphor. It is an arithmetic problem") would cost nothing. No fragment stacks, no em-dashes, no runs of one-sentence paragraphs.

signals.thesis: A cable-news-captured congregation is a formation problem, not an argument problem; the pastor cannot out-shout forty hours with forty minutes, so he must name the capture rather than the channel, build the counter-liturgy of the table, and first admit he stands in the same current.
stockPhrases: Here is where many of us go wrong
unverifiable: Hauerwas & Willimon, Resident Aliens: "The church doesn't have a social strategy. The church is a social strategy." — the idea is genuinely theirs and the book is real, but verify the verbatim wording and punctuation before it stands in quotation marks

essay:preaching-to-a-divided-room.title: How to Preach to a Politically Divided Church
essay:preaching-to-a-divided-room.notes: The thinking is sound and the sources are real (Finally Comes the Poet is correctly dated 1989; Acts 20:27, 2 Timothy 4:2, 2 Samuel 12 all check against ESV), and the Nathan section is the best material here because it refuses to make indirection a technique ("The story was a way in, not a way out"). But the gait is the old one: thirteen "Not X. Y." turns plus paired antitheses ("Preach to the position and you get a fight. Preach to the fear and you get a hearing"; "If they can predict it, you have a tribe. If they cannot, you may have a pulpit"), the fragment stack "The whole counsel. Not the comfortable counsel. Not the half that plays well with the donors," and outline signposts ("Here is the discipline that holds the whole thing together," "The last thing, and the most pastoral," "Study what Nathan did, because it is everything"). The fear section is schematically symmetrical ("The man who has gone rigid about the border... The woman who has gone rigid the other way"), exactly the perfect-symmetry the standard flags. The closing paragraph gathers every prior section into one long restatement rather than landing a new weight; the real ending is the earlier "in his own body, on a Friday." Self-implication is genuine ("I have preached the sermon that flattered my own instincts and called it courage").

signals.thesis: Preaching to a politically sorted room means declaring the whole counsel, speaking as Brueggemann's poet who dissolves the two-team frame rather than arguing inside it, following Nathan's indirection-then-verdict, wounding only from inside the wound, and preaching to the fear beneath the position.
stockPhrases: Here is the discipline that holds the whole thing together
The last thing, and the most pastoral.
Study what Nathan did, because it is everything.
This is the key the divided room hands us
unverifiable: "a preacher who could say *we have all sinned*" — italicized as a quotation with no speaker or reference; it is not Romans 3:23 verbatim and is unanchored

essay:the-last-nonpartisan-in-the-room.title: Should Pastors Stay Politically Neutral?
essay:the-last-nonpartisan-in-the-room.notes: The load-bearing distinction is real and well drawn ("There are matters on which silence is faithfulness, and there are matters on which silence is the betrayal"), Galatians 2 and John 17 are quoted accurately with references, and the ending earns its weight by passing through the cross ("driven outside every camp and crucified between two thieves precisely so that no camp could claim him"). But the register is antithesis as default gait: fourteen "Not X. Y." turns ("That is not the calling. That is cowardice wearing the calling's clothes"; "That is not a sentimental thought. It is a tactical one"), and the structure repeats itself and admits it in a heading ("The counterfeit and the real thing, one more time"). "Both sides run the same play with the same vocabulary" is the perfect-symmetry move the standard warns against, and the essay's hero is its intended reader, the nonpartisan pastor "standing exactly where he should be," with self-implication limited to one clause ("a counterfeit... I have seen in my own heart") and a final flick at everyone else ("still auditioning for a tribe"), which risks the flattery loop for the pastor audience. Signposts "Here is what holds," "Now the correction," "Watch how the pressure actually arrives" are outline language.

signals.thesis: The pastor who refuses partisan capture is neither neutral nor cowardly but a man whose deepest loyalty is already spent on Christ; he confronts like Paul at Antioch where the gospel is at stake, refuses conscription where it is not, guards the unity of John 17, and bears a loneliness that is the shape of Christ's own belonging.
stockPhrases: Here is what holds.
Now the correction, because the previous point is where the cowardice hides
Watch how the pressure actually arrives
one more time
unverifiable: Eugene Peterson "wrote often about the isolation of the pastoral vocation" — no book or passage named; a soft attribution doing decorative work

essay:when-elders-are-loyal-to-a-party.title: When Your Church Leaders Serve a Party First
essay:when-elders-are-loyal-to-a-party.notes: The steelman is honest ("the men involved are usually not villains... the most committed people in the church"), the vote-versus-qualification distinction is the best practical clarity in the batch ("You are not questioning a man's vote. You are holding an officer of the church to the qualifications of his office"), self-implication is concrete ("caught myself in a leaders' meeting assuming a brother's spiritual seriousness from the way he votes"), and the ending passes through the Chief Shepherd and Peter's own restoration. Two failures. First, a citation error the argument leans on repeatedly: the essay quotes Titus 1:7 as "not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome," but that wording is 1 Timothy 3:3; Titus 1:7 reads "not arrogant or quick-tempered or a drunkard or violent or greedy for gain," so every later appeal to "the Titus 1 standard" on quarrelsomeness rests on the wrong reference. Second, fifteen "Not X. Y." turns in 2,500 words ("A shepherd who will only feed the sheep that vote his way is not a shepherd. He is a partisan with a title"; "Your job is not to win the board. Your job is to keep that appearing in front of it"), plus "The lesson for a pastor is twofold and both halves matter. First... Second," which is sermon-outline language. Fix the reference, thin the antitheses, and this ships.

signals.thesis: A politically captured elder board is a character problem the New Testament qualifications already name; the pastor forms his elders as he forms his people, confronts on gospel grounds like Paul at Antioch when he must, and in the hardest case re-forms the board, never on partisan grounds.
stockPhrases: So what is the actual work.
The lesson for a pastor is twofold and both halves matter. First... Second
Honesty requires naming the hardest case
unverifiable: Titus 1:7 quoted as "above reproach . . . not arrogant or quick-tempered . . . not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome" — "not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome" is 1 Timothy 3:3 (ESV), not Titus 1:7; the reference is wrong and the essay's repeated "Titus 1" appeals to quarrelsomeness inherit the error

essay:burnout-is-not-a-badge.title: Why Do Pastors Treat Exhaustion as Faithfulness?
essay:burnout-is-not-a-badge.notes: Correct against the old register and wrong against the current one. Twenty "Not X. Y." constructions in 2,200 words is the gait, not a hinge ("It is not a medal. It is a wound"; "The empty man is not the faithful man. He is just empty"; "This is not humility. It is a quiet blasphemy"; "Not a consultant. A brother"), and the piece thinks in fragment stacks ("Busy. Slammed. Haven't had a day off in weeks"; "Where did we get this. Not from Scripture. We will get to Scripture"; "God rested. Who do we think we are"). The bolded "theology problem wearing a scheduling problem's clothes" is a stock construction that recurs across the corpus ("cowardice wearing the calling's clothes" in the nonpartisan essay). The thinking underneath is real: Weber's worldly asceticism is correctly placed, the congregation is treated fairly ("No one in the building is a villain"), the board section refuses the self-care evasion, and the self-implication is specific ("I have measured my own seriousness by my fatigue"). The Sabbath quotation is italicized as Scripture but is not verbatim ESV and carries no reference. The ending lands and passes through repentance ("What does repentance look like here. It looks like taking the day"), but is delivered as verdict-stack rather than a developed close.

signals.thesis: The church has turned pastoral exhaustion into a moral badge, a Christian heresy with a Protestant pedigree, when Scripture treats depletion as a wound to be healed; repentance means taking the actual Sabbath and refusing to praise exhaustion in one another.
stockPhrases: And here is the part the badge hides.
So let us be plain about what burnout actually is.
I want to be plain about why
a theology problem wearing a scheduling problem's clothes
unverifiable: "Six days you shall labor, but the seventh is a Sabbath" — italicized as Scripture but not verbatim ESV (Exodus 20:9-10 reads "Six days you shall labor, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God"); no reference given
Weber "writing in 1905" and "treated rest as suspect and idleness as the gravest sin" — the book is real (1904-05) and the gloss is defensible, but no primary passage is named

essay:the-loneliest-room-in-the-church.title: Why Are Pastors So Lonely in a Full Church?
essay:the-loneliest-room-in-the-church.notes: The middle of this essay is genuinely developed prose and the best writing in the batch on its subject: the vault image is sustained ("He adds to it every week and subtracts from it never"), the marriage paragraph refuses the easy answer with real tenderness ("She is a gift and she is not a colleague"), the confidentiality objection is steelmanned before it is answered, and the self-implication is specific and costly ("I sent him an encouraging text instead of driving over... I had done almost nothing"). Bellah's Habits of the Heart is correctly dated 1985 and Peterson's tenure is accurate. But thirteen "Not X. Y." turns and three list-fragment stacks ("The affair the husband confessed... The diagnosis the family asked you to keep. The doubt the elder whispered"; "Another pastor who will hear the doubt without flinching. A confessor under genuine seal. A friendship...") pull it back toward the old gait. The closing line invents a specific the text does not supply: "He was sitting forty miles from seven thousand who would have known his name" has no basis in 1 Kings 19, and a plausible-sounding number is exactly the fabrication the standard forbids. The essay also shares its Elijah scaffold and its PCN-pitch penultimate section with two other essays in this cluster, and the ending is a callback that never passes through Christ.

signals.thesis: Pastoral loneliness is the loneliness of the full room, confidential weight that only ever comes in and never goes out, made worse by a church that dismantled the historic structures of care; the remedy is one safe person who can hear the weight without the details.
stockPhrases: I want to say something to the pastor reading this
I want to be careful here, because the obvious objection is real
This is, in plain terms, why the Pastors Connection Network exists
unverifiable: "sitting forty miles from seven thousand" — no textual basis for forty miles in 1 Kings 19; an invented specific
Eugene Peterson paragraph ("saw the pastorate clearly enough to describe the parts no one wanted described") — paraphrase with no book named
"The church growth movement of the 1970s and 80s remade the pastor as a CEO" — defensible history but no source named

essay:the-pastor-nobody-checks-on.title: Who Pastors the Pastor When No One Checks In?
essay:the-pastor-nobody-checks-on.notes: The grammar metaphor is a real idea carried through ("He is the subject of the verb. He is rarely its object"), the history paragraph does honest work (desert fathers, anam cara, Puritan brethren), the reason care must come from outside the congregation is argued rather than asserted ("He cannot fall apart in front of the people who decide whether to renew his contract"), and the turn on the pastor's own complicity is the strongest self-implication in the cluster ("a man can prefer the familiar starvation to the unfamiliar exposure. I have made that preference. I know its taste"). But it is written in the old register: thirteen "Not X. Y." turns, fragment stacks used as argument ("Not how the building campaign was going. Not whether attendance had recovered. How they were"; "The body before the assignment. The care before the rebuke"), and a two-line verdict ending ("Somebody fed Elijah. Nobody is feeding him") that lands but is exactly the choppy close the standard ranks below a developed one. "The research says so" is an unnamed authority propping a factual claim. Elijah under the broom tree with "I, even I only, am left" and the seven thousand appears here, in the loneliest-room essay, and in burnout-is-not-a-badge, each time as the hinge; the cluster is recycling one scaffold. Scripture quotations (1 Kings 19:4, 19:7) are accurate ESV, though the citations are dropped mid-sentence without terminal punctuation.

signals.thesis: Pastoral loneliness is the designed output of a vocation in which care runs one direction; the historic church kept the shepherd under care, so someone outside the congregation must reverse the arrow, and the pastor must stop holding the door shut from the inside.
stockPhrases: This is not an anomaly. It is the design.
This is worth saying plainly to ourselves.
I will say it plainly because I have watched it work
You know who he is. You might be him.
unverifiable: "Most pastors do not have one such relationship. The research says so" — no study named
Brigid of Kildare on the anam cara ("a body without a head") — hedged as tradition, which is acceptable, but it is a secondhand saying popularized in modern retellings, not a primary text

essay:when-the-calling-costs-more.title: When the Calling Costs More Than They Told You
essay:when-the-calling-costs-more.notes: The central distinction is worth the essay ("The cross of Christ is one thing. The cross your committee handed you may be something else entirely, and conflating the two is how faithful men learn to suffer things God never asked them to suffer"), and the Jethro section turns theology into a Tuesday the way the standard asks ("Prayer is good and prayer is not a substitute for Jethro's spreadsheet"). But the architecture is a sermon outline wearing an essay: "The first move... The second move... The third move... There is a fourth move," which the voice standard names explicitly as a thing to avoid, and the bolded pull-quote repeats the previous paragraph's sentence almost verbatim. Fourteen "Not X. Y." turns and fragment stacks ("Sacrifice. Surrender. The narrow road"; "Not weak men. Good ones"; "Count it now. The real number, not the brochure") set the old gait. Not one Scripture reference travels with a quotation, and the Jeremiah line ("But it was in my heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with holding it in, and I could not") matches neither ESV nor KJV verbatim; "the survey work says the same thing" is an unnamed authority. The elder board and committee are the villains here without a strongest-case hearing ("a system that found it cheaper to spend his family than to staff his church"), and the writer stays mostly in the observer's chair ("I have watched this gap break good men"), entering only through "we" and a named fear rather than a named failure. The ending is a ledger callback with weight but no passage through Christ.

signals.thesis: The cost of ministry was sold as an abstraction and arrives itemized; much of what breaks pastors is not the cross but structure the church built and baptized, and telling the two apart is work a man cannot do from inside his own fatigue.
stockPhrases: The first move... The second move... The third move... There is a fourth move
Read that as the diagnosis it is.
Notice what Jethro did not do, because it is the move we have lost.
unverifiable: Jeremiah 20:9 quoted as "But it was in my heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with holding it in, and I could not" — verbatim in neither ESV nor KJV; no reference given
"Two thousand years later the survey work says the same thing" — no study named

No Scripture reference accompanies any quotation in the essay (Luke 14, Jeremiah 20, 2 Corinthians 11:28, 1 Timothy 5:18, Galatians 6:6, Exodus 18:17-18, Mark 1:35-38 all quoted or paraphrased unreferenced)

essay:why-pastors-quit.title: Why Pastors Quit
essay:why-pastors-quit.notes: The thinking is real and the Elijah material stays with the image long enough to do work ("God does not rebuke the suicidal prophet... The body restored before the commission renewed"), the steelman aside on leaving-as-wisdom is honest, and the self-implication is concrete ("I have watched a brother drain out slowly and done nothing but pray for him from a comfortable distance"). But the register is the old gait: roughly a dozen "Not X. Y." turns in 2,200 words ("It is not the weight. It is the solitude under the weight"; "Loneliness is not a side effect of the attrition. It is the engine of it"; "He does not quit the calling. He quits the substitute"), plus intra-paragraph fragment runs ("No puncture. No bang."; "Company. The thing he was missing. The thing that would have kept him from the tree.") and the listed-wounds stack ("The board meeting where... The salary conversation... The criticism... The family..."). "I am inside this indictment, brothers" is the house rule quoted back as prose, and it recurs verbatim in another essay in this batch. The Barna figure (around four in ten) matches the 2021-22 releases and is hedged responsibly, but the "deeper finding" that the most isolated are most likely to leave is attributed to the research without a locatable source. Cut two-thirds of the antitheses, keep the two bolded verdicts, and this ships.

signals.thesis: Pastors quit not from an event but from an erosion whose engine is isolation, and the cure is what God gave Elijah under the broom tree: rest, bread, and a companion.
stockPhrases: Here is the hard mercy in all of it
So let us name what actually drains the tire
This is the answer hiding inside the diagnosis
I am inside this indictment, brothers
This is the pattern, and every pastor who has lived it recognizes it
That is the grief and the hope in the same sentence
unverifiable: Barna: 'the pastors most likely to leave are the ones most isolated, the ones with no close friend in ministry' — presented as the research's deeper finding without a specific release; the four-in-ten headline checks against Barna 2021-22 but this claim does not travel with a source
Peterson paraphrase (pastor pulled from cure of souls into running a religious business) — unquoted and fair to The Contemplative Pastor, but no work is named

essay:emotional-labor-in-marriage.title: When One Spouse Carries the Marriage Alone
essay:emotional-labor-in-marriage.notes: Nearest to a pass in this batch: the argument accumulates in the standard's order (the hundred articles, "The describing is accurate. The blaming is where most of it goes wrong," the distinction between undone and unseen, the non-seeing spouse given his honest form in "He is not lazy. She is not nagging," then Martha, Hochschild, and a concrete confession: "the half I could point to was the easy half"). Sources check: Hochschild's The Second Shift is 1989, Luke 10:40 and Galatians 6:2 are verbatim ESV, and the ending passes through repentance ("the seeing itself, late as it is, is the beginning of repentance") before it presses the conscience. What keeps it from shipping as it stands: "So here is the claim I will spend the rest of this essay on" is signposting the standard forbids; the undone/unseen antithesis is stated three separate times; every one of five sections opens on a one-sentence paragraph, a mechanical pattern; and the closing mold ("The mental load does not need a medal. It needs a witness.") is the same template as the drift essay's "The vineyard does not need a hero. It needs a keeper." Proverbs 31:27 is rendered "watching over the ways of her household," which is not the ESV's "looks well to the ways." A light pass: cut the signpost, one of the three restatements, and two section-opener one-liners.

signals.thesis: The management labor in a marriage is invisible by design, so the injury is not that it went undone but that it went unseen, and repair must begin with seeing before any chore chart.
stockPhrases: So here is the claim I will spend the rest of this essay on
That last part is the whole problem
I have to stop describing now and confess
Everything else is logistics
unverifiable: 'watching over the ways of her household (Proverbs 31:27)' — not ESV wording ('looks well to the ways'); a blend of translations offered as if verbatim
'a civilization that spent three centuries agreeing the work was not real' — a gestured span with no event or source behind it

essay:fighting-fair-is-not-enough.title: Why Fighting Fair Isn't Enough to Save a Marriage
essay:fighting-fair-is-not-enough.notes: The opening concedes honestly ("These are good rules. I have taught versions of them, and I would teach them again") and the repair-attempt paragraph is the best material, but from the second section on the essay runs on aphorism after aphorism: "Civility is not communion," "You cannot audit your way to intimacy," "the marriage is already in hospice," "Fairness divides. Grace binds," roughly sixteen "Not X. Y." turns and a perfectly symmetrical fairness/grace section ("Fairness keeps the books... Grace burns the ledger") — several attempted slogans where the standard wants one earned verdict. Self-implication is present but abstract ("the case is the last thing standing between me and the admission that I, too, am part of the problem"). Two citation problems: "Love... keeps no record of wrongs" (1 Corinthians 13:5) is NIV in quotation marks with no translation named (ESV reads "it is not irritable or resentful"), and "Augustine called it incurvatus in se" attributes Luther's Latin coinage to Augustine. Gottman is credited here with repair as "the single thing that most predicts" survival, while the resentment essay credits him with contempt as "the strongest predictor of divorce"; the platform cannot have both. The ending does pass through death and resurrection, but the last paragraph recaps before it lands.

signals.thesis: Fair-fighting rules are a floor mistaken for a ceiling; marriages die less of unfair fighting than of two people who fought clean and never surrendered, and only grace that drops the case reaches what the rules cannot.
stockPhrases: This is the trap
This reframes everything
There is a tell for this
Paul saw the deeper game and named it without flinching
rearranging deck chairs on the actual battle
by an order of magnitude
unverifiable: 'Love... keeps no record of wrongs' (1 Corinthians 13:5) — NIV wording quoted as if default; ESV reads 'it is not irritable or resentful'
'Augustine called it incurvatus in se' — the Latin phrase is Luther's (Romans lectures) developing Augustine's idea; attribution as stated is inaccurate

Gottman: 'The single thing that most predicts whether a marriage survives... is whether they repair' — overstated; Gottman's most-cited single predictor is contempt, which the resentment essay in this batch claims instead

essay:forgiveness-without-pretending.title: How Do You Forgive Without Pretending It Didn't Happen?
essay:forgiveness-without-pretending.notes: The distinctions are the right ones and pastorally necessary, especially the reconciliation section that keeps the endangered spouse visible ("You can fully forgive a debt and still decline to extend a new line of credit"), and the confession is real ("I am the man holding the receipt more often than I want to admit"). But the thesis is restated at least four times in nearly identical form ("Real forgiveness is not the minimizing of a wound"; "Forgiveness is not the minimizing of a wrong. It is the opposite"; "Full naming, then full release"; "You were never asked to pretend it did not happen. You were asked to forgive that it did"), around fifteen "Not X. Y." turns carry the gait, and the penultimate paragraph is an imperative stack that recaps the whole argument ("So stop pretending. Name the wound... Absorb the cost. Die the small death."). "And here is the thing we least want to hear" is the forbidden phrase itself. "Seventy times seven" is not the ESV ("seventy-seven times"), and the absorb-the-cost framing is Keller's and Volf's, which is fine to use but reads as if the writer's own discovery ("That is what it actually is, underneath the religious language"). Romans 5:8, Genesis 50:20, and Colossians 3:13 are verbatim and doing work.

signals.thesis: Real forgiveness requires naming the wound at full weight and then absorbing its cost yourself; it is distinct from reconciliation, which requires the offender's repentance.
stockPhrases: And here is the thing we least want to hear
That sentence is the receipt
This is the part we skip
denial wearing a halo
Those are not the same, and the difference is the whole thing
unverifiable: 'seventy times seven (Matthew 18:21–22)' — ESV reads 'seventy-seven times'; the KJV/NASB rendering is used without naming it

essay:protecting-marriage-in-ministry.title: When Ministry Is Quietly Killing Your Marriage
essay:protecting-marriage-in-ministry.notes: The mechanism is named with precision the standard asks for ("The very holiness of the reason is what gags the people it is costing. They cannot protest without sounding like they are protesting God"), Song of Solomon 1:6 is quoted exactly and counted correctly at fifteen words, Luke 5:15-16 does real work, and the self-implication is specific ("I have come home from the labor of God too depleted for the labor of love, and I have called my depletion holy"). The register is the failure: roughly eighteen "Not X. Y." turns ("The demands did not arrive as temptation. They arrived as duty"; "The home is not the warm-up for the ministry. The home is the ministry's credential"; "Your spouse is not a competitor to your calling. Your spouse is the first congregation"), fragment runs ("So you go. And you go."; "It will never tell you to stop. That is not the church's job. It is yours."), the same verdict landed twice ("A depleted man follows the affirmation every time" and "a tired man follows the loud thing"), and "I am inside this indictment, not above it," the house phrase repeated verbatim from the pastors essay. Peterson's "busy pastor is a lazy pastor" is a self-diagnosis in The Contemplative Pastor ("I am busy because I am lazy"), not the insult the essay says he meant. No steelman of the congregation's real claim beyond "the need is genuinely endless." The ending is earned: it returns to the vineyard and the withdrawing Christ.

signals.thesis: Ministry kills marriages by disguising neglect as duty, and the boundary that protects the home is not a scheduling trick but an act of obedience to a prior calling.
stockPhrases: I am inside this indictment, not above it
This is the trap with a halo on it
the load-bearing wall of the whole structure
So how do you keep your own vineyard while keeping the Lord's
The boundary is the obedience
unverifiable: 'He called the busy pastor a lazy pastor, and he meant it as an insult' — Peterson's line is self-directed ('I am busy because I am lazy'); the framing as an insult aimed at others is a distortion, not a fabrication

essay:the-covenant-you-didnt-understand.title: What Are You Really Promising in Your Marriage Vows?
essay:the-covenant-you-didnt-understand.notes: The strongest thinking in the batch: the contract is given its honest form ("That is not cynicism. That is what a contract is for"), the abuse caveat is placed before the argument rather than after it ("the people who most need the high view of covenant are also the people most likely to have it used against them"), Genesis 15:17, Malachi 2:14, and 2 Timothy 2:13 are verbatim ESV and structural, and Hauerwas is paraphrased fairly. Two failures. First, the writer never enters the indictment: he is the observer throughout ("I have watched couples discover," "I have sat with these marriages"), and the one "we" ("We just smuggled it in afterward, quietly, in the privacy of our own disappointment") is where a husband should have said what terms and conditions he brought to his own altar. Second, roughly eighteen "Not X. Y." turns ("That was not a failure of your wedding. It is the nature of a covenant"; "You did not promise to love your spouse as long as they earned it. You promised to love them"; "You are not the foundation. You were never strong enough to be the foundation") make antithesis the gait even inside developed paragraphs. "The source code of every marriage that survives" is the machine's metaphor, not a pastor's. The ending is earned and passes through the cross.

signals.thesis: Struggling marriages fail because two people made a covenant while believing it was a contract; a covenant has no exit clause because God walked between the pieces alone, and His faithfulness, not theirs, holds it.
stockPhrases: This is not decoration. This is the structure
the source code of every marriage that survives
The difference that changes everything
Those are not the same loss
unverifiable: 'The word translated companion means the one you were knit to, allied with, bound to' (Malachi 2:14) — the Hebrew is a form of chaver, companion/associate; 'knit to' is a gloss the lexicon does not supply

essay:the-resentment-in-your-marriage.title: What the Resentment in Your Marriage Is Telling You
essay:the-resentment-in-your-marriage.notes: The grievance/contempt distinction is precise and the two-sided work section is fair to both spouses ("The competence of the person beside you has been subsidizing your peace, and you have been spending the subsidy without reading the statement"). But this is the heaviest tic-load short of the drift essay: about twenty "Not X. Y." turns ("You are not screaming. You are counting"; "Not the explosion. The sentence"; "It is not the rot. It is the symptom"), the smoke-alarm metaphor stated three times, the Ephesians 4:26 point made twice in consecutive sentences ("He is not asking you to feel less" / "The instruction is not to feel less"), a section heading repeated verbatim as its own first sentence ("So the work is two-sided, and neither side gets to skip theirs"), and the closing is a recap ending on a proverb cliché ("the second-best time is tonight"). Self-implication is a hedge, not an entry: "I have felt the edge of it, which is the only reason I can write about it honestly" names nothing. Scripture is stretched twice: Hebrews 12:17 is about Esau's birthright, not bitterness that "had already chosen for him," and Ephesians 4:26 is addressed to the church, so "the only piece of marriage counsel in Scripture" is loose. The second section also compresses the emotional-labor essay's whole argument (invisible labor, the unthanked ledger) into three paragraphs; the two pieces overlap enough that a reader of both hears the same essay twice.

signals.thesis: Resentment is not the disease but distorted information, a fairness claim gone underground, and marriages survive it by speaking it as a request before it hardens into contempt.
stockPhrases: So here is the claim
recognizing it is half the battle
the second-best time is tonight
This is the marriage's quiet economy
That is the whole difference, and it is decided by whether you speak
unverifiable: Hebrews 12:17 applied to hardened bitterness ('his bitterness had already chosen for him') — the text concerns Esau's sold birthright; the resentment reading is imported
'the only piece of marriage counsel in Scripture that addresses the mechanism directly' (Ephesians 4:26) — the verse is addressed to the church body, not to marriage
'how long will I bear this in my soul' (Psalm 13:2) — loose paraphrase of ESV 'How long must I take counsel in my soul'; italicized, not quoted, but sits beside the reference as if verbatim

essay:the-slow-drift-that-ends-marriages.title: Why Do Married Couples Slowly Drift Apart?
essay:the-slow-drift-that-ends-marriages.notes: The sound thinking is here (the fever/disease distinction, shamar held long enough to work, the drifter's self-account given fairly in "providing is the same as presence," and a concrete confession: "the email over the eyes across the room, the productive evening over the unproductive conversation that was actually the marriage"). The theological paragraph on God turning toward a turning-away people is the essay's real verdict and should be its ending. Instead the register is the worst in the batch: roughly twenty-seven "Not X. Y." turns ("Most marriages do not die from a wound. They die from a draft"; "You did not stop loving your spouse. You stopped turning toward them"; "Not scandal. Not enemy"; "you are no longer guarding. You are rebuilding"), the phrase "with a clear conscience the whole way down" used verbatim twice, a recap final paragraph, and a closing mold ("The vineyard does not need a hero. It needs a keeper") identical in shape to the emotional-labor essay's last line. Two overclaims: "Drift is the spiritual condition Jesus named most often" is asserted, not shown, and the wicked servant of Matthew 24:48-49 does not begin "gradually, without ever deciding to"; the text has him beating his fellow servants. Bellah is fairly paraphrased but "the slow replacement of covenant with arrangement" is the essay's phrase wearing Habits of the Heart's attribution.

signals.thesis: Most marriages end not by a wound but by drift, thousands of small turnings-away that never felt like decisions, and drift is undone only by the same small turnings toward, modeled on God's daily faithfulness to a drifting people.
stockPhrases: This is the lie at the center of it
Consider how it actually works
That is precisely the point
with a clear conscience the whole way down (used twice)
There is a deeper reason the small turnings are the only cure, and it is theological rather than practical
The vineyard does not need a hero. It needs a keeper.
unverifiable: 'Drift is the spiritual condition Jesus named most often and the church preaches least' — an unsupported superlative

Matthew 24:48–49: 'begins, gradually, without ever deciding to, to live as though no one is coming home' — the gradualness is imported; the text says the servant beats his fellow servants and eats with drunkards

Bellah et al., Habits of the Heart (1985): 'They called it the language of the therapeutic, the slow replacement of covenant with arrangement' — the therapeutic ethos is theirs; the covenant/arrangement phrasing is the essay's, presented as their term

essay:what-silence-costs-a-marriage.title: What Silence Actually Costs a Marriage
essay:what-silence-costs-a-marriage.notes: The argument accumulates instead of asserting: the familiar account ("We treat it as neutral"), the concession ("Sometimes a couple has stopped fighting because they have genuinely made peace"), the distinction (rest vs. hiding, tested by "whether there is anything you have decided not to say"), then Genesis 3 held long enough to govern the whole piece and returned to at the close. Self-implication is concrete and unforced: "So I have, more than once, chosen the silence, told myself it was grace and patience... and known in some honest interior room that it was just fear in better clothing." Scripture is verbatim and doing work (Gen 3:9, Ps 32:3, Heb 12:15, Eph 4:15), and the ending passes through God's pursuit and leaves weight rather than resolving it. Roughly eight "not X, it is Y" turns and a verdict closing most paragraphs ("The calm is real. So is the cause of death.") are residue of the old gait, but they sit inside developed paragraphs and never outnumber the argument; trimming two or three would help and is not blocking. One citation to confirm before it ships: the Bonhoeffer paraphrase is loose and should be checked against the confession chapter of Life Together or softened to "wrote about."

signals.thesis: Two silences look identical from across the room; the hiding kind, born when Adam went quiet in the garden, is what kills a marriage, and love breaks it the way God did, by walking toward it and asking "Where are you?"
unverifiable: Bonhoeffer, Life Together (1939), 'said that the breaking of silence is one of the hardest and most necessary acts of love, because real fellowship refuses to let a brother sink alone into the isolation of his own heart' — offered as paraphrase; the direction matches the confession chapter, but this wording is not his; confirm or soften

'The Gottman research... found it among the strongest predictors of divorce, more telling than anger, more telling than the frequency of conflict' — no study named; consistent with the Four Horsemen work but unspecific

essay:what-the-bible-says-about-submissi.title: What the Bible Really Says About Submission in Marriage
essay:what-the-bible-says-about-submissi.notes: The exegesis is largely sound and the objection paragraph ("has the structure not simply dissolved into a slogan that means whatever the reader wants") is the right move, but the register is the old one: a one-word paragraph "To die.", standalone slogan lines ("Submission is what you give. It is never what you take."; "The cross is the only definition of headship Scripture gives."), and a dozen antitheses stacked into competing metaphors, "not a ladder. It is a stretcher," "not a command center. It is a nervous system," "It is not the right to be served. It is the obligation to be spent." The standard asks for one earned verdict, not four. Fairness is thin where it matters: the rank-reading of v. 21 is dismissed in a parenthesis as "code for 'some submit to others according to rank,'" which no complementarian exegete would sign, and "I want to be fair to readers who hold a complementarian reading" arrives after the verdict has landed. Self-implication is present but generic ("I will not pretend I have always read it well"), and "the Bible has a different word for that, and it is not approving" names no word. The manuscript claim (no verb in v. 22 in the earliest witnesses) is defensible and the Bonhoeffer listening passage is accurately paraphrased.

signals.thesis: Read from verse 21 rather than 22, Ephesians 5 addresses wives as agents, hands the husband the heavier command (to die), and defines headship by the cross, so any reading that leaves the husband comfortable and the wife small inverts the text.
stockPhrases: So let us go back and read the thing slowly, because almost no one does
My claim is plain, and the rest of this essay is me grounding it in the text
To die. (one-word paragraph as dramatic hook)
Say it in a room of Christians and watch the faces close.
unverifiable: 'the Bible has a different word for that [subjugation], and it is not approving' — no word given; vague claim presented as textual fact
'one of the most sexually broken cities in the empire' (Corinth) — popular-preaching trope, overstated relative to scholarship on Roman Corinth
'Aristotle had written one' (a household code) — Politics I treats household rule; acceptable but loosely stated
'spends roughly three times as many words' to husbands — roughly right for 5:25–33 vs 5:22–24; stated as if measured

essay:when-marriage-becomes-a-mirror.title: When Marriage Becomes a Mirror
essay:when-marriage-becomes-a-mirror.notes: Every source checks (Aristophanes in the Symposium, Abba Moses's 'sit in your cell,' Gen 3:7, Eph 5:26, Prov 27:6, Eccl 4:9–10, Gary Thomas's Sacred Marriage question), and the self-implication is real: "I have heard a true word about myself from across a kitchen and chosen, in the half-second I had, to defend the lie instead of receive the word." But the piece is built almost entirely from antithesis, some fifteen "not X. Y." turns: "Marriage does not create these things. It reveals them." "The source is not Genesis. The source is Plato's Symposium." "Not who you intended to be. Who you are." "The opposite of love in a marriage is not anger. It is the decision to no longer be known." Paragraph after paragraph closes on a punch ("It is faster. It costs nothing now. It costs everything later."), which is exactly the default gait the standard retires. The thesis is asserted in the first two sentences and illustrated rather than accumulated toward. The closing "Someone saw it first, and stayed" is earned, but the paragraph before it recaps the opening ("You did not marry a stranger. You married a mirror"), and the piece shares its 'corpse' and hiding-behind-the-tree images with the silence essay; read together they sound like one pattern rather than one man.

signals.thesis: Marriage does not complete you; it exposes you, and the exposure is God's instrument of sanctification, bearable only because you were already seen all the way down and kept by Him.
stockPhrases: I want to say something before we go any further
Here is what the Bible actually says happened
It is faster. It costs nothing now. It costs everything later.

essay:when-you-married-someone-you-no-lo.title: When You No Longer Recognize the Person You Married
essay:when-you-married-someone-you-no-lo.notes: The strongest thinking in the marriage set: grief vs. grievance ("Grievance has a target. Grief just sits in your chest"), the Genesis 15 covenant preceding the people it will hold, Taylor's age of authenticity conceded before it is challenged ("It is not all wrong. But it is acid on a marriage"), and an honest turn inward: "you also became a stranger... That is a harder question, and it indicts me first." But the register is old: seventeen antitheses ("You did not fall for a statue. You fell for a fire"; "The resentment feels like fidelity. It is the opposite"), sections opened with one-line hooks ("Scripture is not romantic about this."), and an ending that is pure recap, two one-sentence paragraphs repeating the bolded thesis: "The stranger in your kitchen is not the death of the marriage. / The stranger is the person the marriage is for." "So here is the claim, and the rest of this is me earning it" is the same signposting formula the submission essay uses. "hypomenei is a military word. It means to hold the position" is decorative Greek and overstated (the word means to remain or endure), and Abram "laughed at the promise" after the Genesis 15 covenant and after his renaming, so the sequence is off.

signals.thesis: The spouse who has become a stranger is not the marriage's failure but its purpose; the covenant was a promise to every person they would become, and the work is to learn them again.
stockPhrases: So here is the claim, and the rest of this is me earning it
This is the moment most people misread, and they misread it the same way.
Scripture is not romantic about this.
persons are verbs
unverifiable: 'The Greek word for endure, hypomenei, is a military word. It means to hold the position' — hypomenō means to remain/endure; it has military uses in classical Greek but is not 'a military word'; overstated decorative Greek
Abram as 'the one who laughed at the promise' bound in Genesis 15 — the laugh is Genesis 17:17, after the covenant and after the renaming to Abraham; sequence is wrong

essay:discipline-without-domination.title: How to Discipline Without Crushing Your Child
essay:discipline-without-domination.notes: The repair section is the best material in the parenting set ("The child has watched authority humble itself... the precise opposite of domination and the exact shape of the gospel"), and Hebrews 12, Ephesians 6:4, and Holland's Dominion (2019) do real work. Three things need fixing. The Bonhoeffer attribution ("it is always easier to dominate than to suffer the slow labor of love") has no locatable source and reads as decoration; cut it or find the text. The Proverbs handling is evasive: dismissing 'spare the rod' by its Hudibras origin while Proverbs 13:24 says nearly the same thing, and declaring the rod "the shepherd's instrument... not a weapon" when Proverbs 23:13–14 speaks of striking with it, presents a contested reading as settled, and no defender of traditional discipline would sign it. And a father of five writing about yelling at a child never says 'I'; the indictment stops at "when we are honest, it is serving us," which for this author on this subject is the missed hinge. Sixteen antitheses ("The failure named is formation. The failure denied is the wound."), a refrain used twice ("The gap is small. Everything is in it."), "Read that again," and a section headed 'The verdict' that restates the second paragraph three ways are the old gait.

signals.thesis: Most discipline is the parent's anger discharged in the costume of correction; discipline serves the child's eventual self-government while domination serves the parent, and the repair after a failure teaches more than the failure cost.
stockPhrases: Read that again, because the accusation of softness is the thing that keeps the throne standing
Here is the mercy the angry parent forgets in the shame afterward
## The verdict (section heading, sermon-outline template shared with three other essays)
The gap is small. Everything is in it. (refrain used twice)
