John 20:27 rendered 'Put your finger here. See my hands. Reach out your hand and put it in my side' is not ESV verbatim ('Put your finger here, and see my hands; and put out your hand, and place it in my side')
'Why do you hide your face? How long must I wrestle with my thoughts?' splices Psalm 44:24 with NIV Psalm 13:2 (ESV: 'How long must I take counsel in my soul')
The apostles-would-not-die-for-a-lie argument sits next to Tom Holland's name in a way that implies Dominion makes it; Holland's argument is about moral inheritance, not martyrdom as evidence

essay:when-fear-rewrites-theology.title: When Fear Starts Rewriting What You Believe
essay:when-fear-rewrites-theology.notes: The 'I have preached the bunker' section is exactly what the standard asks for: 'There were seasons when I read the headlines before I read the Psalms, and the headlines won, and what came out of me on Sunday had the cadence of the gospel and the marrow of dread.' Haidt's elephant and Brueggemann's disorientation are used as mechanisms, not decoration. What fails is the gait: I count about twelve 'Not X. Y.' hinges ('The rider does not steer. The rider explains', 'Not through study. Through dread', 'A church that is afraid does not preach the kingdom. It preaches the bunker', 'We do not see God as he is. We see God as we are braced for him to be'), and the piece ends on two consecutive slogan paragraphs ('We are defending the fear, and calling it the faith' / 'That is not God. That is the elephant, explained') after the real ending has already landed on Mark 9. The clever lines pile up until they perform depth: 'fear with a steeple', 'adrenaline with a theology degree', 'panic that learned to stand up straight'. 'Three hundred times, give or take' is the debunked 365 folk statistic; actual ESV counts of 'do not be afraid'/'fear not' run roughly 80 to 110, and the claim must come out. Genesis 3:10 and 1 John 4:18 are italicized as quotations but condensed rather than verbatim.

signals.thesis: Fear disguises itself as discernment and quietly rewrites a believer's picture of God into a punishing one; the undoing is naming the fear as fear, the company of people who can see it, and the Christ who is not afraid.
stockPhrases: the search bar at two in the morning
This is the trap inside the trap.
That is the elephant, explained.
unverifiable: 'Three hundred times, give or take, the line returns. Do not be afraid' (the 365 claim is a folk statistic; ESV occurrences of the family of phrases are roughly 80-110)
Genesis 3:10 rendered 'I heard you in the garden, and I was afraid, so I hid' is not verbatim (ESV: 'I heard the sound of you in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself')
1 John 4:18 rendered 'Perfect love casts out fear, because fear has to do with punishment' is a compressed paraphrase presented in italics as quotation

essay:when-god-doesnt-make-sense.title: When God Stops Making Sense
essay:when-god-doesnt-make-sense.notes: The confession is concrete and costs something: 'I have done it... So I explained him. I explained him to people who needed his presence and got my chart instead, and the chart was cold.' Job's friends are steelmanned ('They are not cruel men... They are orthodox men, careful men'), and the senseless-versus-opaque distinction is a real named distinction. But the piece is built from the old kit: five bolded verdicts, about eight 'Not X. Y.' hinges ('It is not evasion. It is God refusing to be reduced to a function', 'He did not get the answer. He got the Answerer', 'The opacity is not in God. It is in the gap'), and 'Read that slowly' is a cousin of 'Let that sink in'. The Charles Taylor buffered-self paragraph sits in the same structural slot with the same opening ('This is harder for us than it was for Job, and Charles Taylor told us why') as the Taylor paragraph in dark-night ('And it is harder for us than it was for John'), which is a template tell. 'A God small enough to be fully explained by you would be a God too small to save you' is presented as Keller pressing a point; it is a variation on Evelyn Underhill's aphorism and should not be laid at Keller's feet without a citation. The closing jab at the atheist's room 'where everything makes sense and no one is home' is a caricature: most unbelievers do not claim the universe makes sense.

signals.thesis: American Christianity sold the faith as an equation (faithfulness in, blessing out); Job shows a God who refuses to be computed, and what the sufferer is given is a presence rather than an explanation.
stockPhrases: Read that slowly.
type the words into the dark
That second room is on offer. It always is.
Stop solving him. Start following him
unverifiable: 'A God small enough to be fully explained by you would be a God too small to save you' attributed to Keller ('Keller pressed exactly this point'); the idea is Evelyn Underhill's ('If God were small enough to be understood, He would not be big enough to be worshipped') and no Keller source is given
Job 42:5 rendered 'I had heard of you with the hearing of the ear' is not ESV verbatim ('by the hearing of the ear')
'a third of the Psalter, by some counts' (hedged; acceptable as hedged)

essay:suffering-without-explanation.title: Why Does God Allow Suffering?
essay:suffering-without-explanation.notes: The argument accumulates properly, the friends are given their due ('They are not villains. They are orthodox'), the theodicies are conceded ('they are not nothing'), and Lewis 1940/1961 and Wolterstorff 1983/1987 are real and doing work. The failures are register and one biography flag. About twelve 'Not X. Y.' hinges ('The later book does not explain. It records', 'They were not malicious. They were anxious', 'The reasons are not for the bereaved. They are for the frightened', 'Not the reason you asked for. The presence you actually needed') plus mirrored symmetry ('The two refusals are the same mercy from two directions'). The bolded 'Let that land on every comforter who ever arrived with a verse and a theory' is 'Let that sink in' in a cassock, and 'here is the thing that should stop us cold' brushes the forbidden 'here's the thing'. 'I have read them carefully and even taught them to students with a clear conscience' extends James's biography beyond the facts on file (pastor, PCN founder); it must be confirmed or cut. The indictment section ('When you tell a grieving mother...') points at 'you' and 'the comforter'; the writer enters only through a general 'Most of us cannot leave the silence alone either', and that is the paragraph where 'I have done this' belongs. The exact Wolterstorff sentence 'God is not only the God of the sufferers but the God who suffers' I could not confirm verbatim; the book's confirmed language is 'the God who suffers with us' and 'Instead of explaining our suffering God shares it'.

signals.thesis: Explanations for suffering do not comfort and usually wound; Job's God refuses to explain and Christ refuses to stay away, and those two refusals are the same mercy.
stockPhrases: Let that land on every comforter
here is the thing that should stop us cold
Here is what I have come to believe
He showed up instead.
unverifiable: 'I have read them carefully and even taught them to students' (biography not on file; confirm or cut)
Wolterstorff quotation 'God is not only the God of the sufferers but the God who suffers' (not confirmed verbatim; confirmed nearby language is 'the God who suffers with us')
'Thirty-seven chapters of being wrong' (the human speeches run roughly Job 3-37, and Job's own speeches are among them; approximate)

essay:the-theology-of-saturday.title: Where Is God on Holy Saturday?
essay:the-theology-of-saturday.notes: This is the most useful thesis in the batch and the Lamentations reading ('The book ends on a Saturday') is genuinely clarifying; the ending refuses cheap hope by name ('I am not going to promise you that your Sunday is coming this week'). But the essay is built on the old rhythm: every section opens with a two-sentence punch ('Notice what Saturday is not. It is not Friday.' / 'The Old Testament has a Saturday book. We do not read it.' / 'We cannot stand Saturday.'), about nine 'Not X. Y.' hinges ('Saturday is not the wound. Saturday is the endless afternoon', 'We are not comforting him. We are refusing to be in the theater with him', 'Not narrating it from Sunday. In it.'), and anaphoric triplets at the close ('He lay in the dark of it. He kept the silence of it. He waited the length of it'; 'The stone is still sealed. The body is still cold. The morning has not come'). The opening paragraph 'Holy Saturday. The day the body lay in the tomb. The day after God died...' is a fragment stack. 'I will not lie about that to make this end gently' appears almost verbatim in the-weight-that-stays, and the two closings share a template ('I am not going to promise... What I can tell you is...'), which is the machine tell the standard warns about. Balthasar's actual term is solidarity with the dead; 'solidarity with the lost' and 'the day God knows what it is to be dead' are the essay's gloss presented as his words, though the piece wisely hedges that the theology is contested. Lamentations 3:22-23 is spliced.

signals.thesis: The church has a theology of Friday and of Sunday but almost none of Holy Saturday, the day most of the grieving actually live in; Lamentations, the descent to the dead, and the disciples' not-knowing show that faith on Saturday is staying in the room.
stockPhrases: Here is what the famous middle of the book is actually doing
Here is the part that should change how we read the whole story
This is the part we will not sit still for
I will not lie about that to make this end gently
unverifiable: Balthasar 'called it the day of God's solidarity with the lost' (his term in Mysterium Paschale is solidarity with the dead; the 'lost' extension is his contested position, but the phrasing is a paraphrase presented as his)
Lamentations 3:22-23 rendered 'his mercies are new every morning; great is your faithfulness' is a splice of the ESV text
The disciples 'sat in a locked room' on Saturday (John 20:19 places the locked doors on Sunday evening; Saturday is inference)

essay:the-weight-that-stays.title: When Grief Doesn't Lift
essay:the-weight-that-stays.notes: The second-Christmas section is the best pastoral writing in the batch, concrete and plausible ('I have sat with people in that second year and watched them apologize for still being sad. Apologize.'), and the Lazarus/1 Thessalonians distinction is exactly the named distinction the standard wants. The essay cannot ship as is because of a misattribution: 'He wrote that grief does not get smaller; we get bigger around it' is credited to Wolterstorff, and it is Lois Tonkin's 1996 'growing around grief' model; the sentence must be reattributed or cut, and the iron-stake image rebuilt around the hole. 'Closure is a real estate term' is glib and inaccurate (closing is the real-estate term; closure entered the vocabulary from Gestalt psychology), and the stage model is caricatured rather than steelmanned; Kubler-Ross herself said the stages were never a hallway. Register: about ten 'Not X. Y.' hinges ('It is not a malfunction of grief. It is what grief is', 'The staying is not the wound failing to heal. The staying is the love refusing to die', 'The grief is not the problem. The lie... that lie is the problem'), an anaphoric 'I will not say... I will not give you... I will not promise' triplet, a fragment triplet 'To remember out loud. To mark the anniversary... To send a note', and the closing 'Not yet. Not on your schedule. But that way, and not the other.' The ending line 'The weight stays. So does he.' is earned but arrives after the same 'I will not lie about it to make this end gently' template used in the-theology-of-saturday. Genesis 37:35 and 1 Thessalonians 4:13 are italicized but not verbatim in any standard translation.

signals.thesis: Grief that does not lift is not a failure but love outliving its object; the resurrection reorients grief rather than removing it, and the church's work is to remember out loud in the years after the casseroles stop.
stockPhrases: They told you it would lift. It did not lift.
I will not lie about it to make this end gently
Closure is a real estate term.
Not yet. Not on your schedule.
unverifiable: 'He wrote that grief does not get smaller; we get bigger around it' attributed to Wolterstorff (this is Lois Tonkin's 1996 'growing around grief' model, not Lament for a Son)
Genesis 37:35 rendered 'I shall go down to my son to the grave mourning' matches no standard translation (ESV: 'I shall go down to Sheol to my son, mourning')
1 Thessalonians 4:13 rendered 'as those who have no hope' is not ESV verbatim ('as others do who have no hope')
'Closure is a real estate term' (closing is the real-estate term; 'closure' as a psychological term comes from Gestalt psychology)

essay:what-psalms-teach-about-anger-at-g.title: Is It Okay to Be Angry at God?
essay:what-psalms-teach-about-anger-at-g.notes: The imprecatory section is the strongest and fairest thing in the batch: 'I am not going to defend the sentiment as a moral instruction... They are not picking up a stone. They are handing the rage to God.' The Brueggemann orientation/disorientation frame is used as mechanism, and the closing 'So was his Son' is one line, earned by the Psalm 22 section. The fairness fails elsewhere: the church's caution is dismissed as 'a verse fired like a warning shot' and later as 'sold to you by people who could not handle a God big enough to be yelled at', without ever engaging why Paul wrote Romans 9:20 or that the same book of Job in which the complainer is commended also has God answering him out of the whirlwind and Job repenting 'in dust and ashes'; a cautious pastor would not sign the account given of him. Self-implication is a church 'we' only ('We taught people that the way to be close to God is to lie to him'); the pastor who has himself said 'be careful with that' never appears, and the section 'The church's instinct is to shush that fury' is where he should. Register: about eleven 'Not X. Y.' hinges ('They are not confessing sin. They are filing a grievance', 'The anger is not a turning away from God. It is the most intense possible turning toward him', 'The psalm is not a permission slip for vengeance. It is the alternative to vengeance'), and the ending stacks three short verdict paragraphs. Psalm 44:23 and Psalm 55:15 are italicized but not ESV verbatim.

signals.thesis: The Psalms canonize anger addressed directly to God; lament and even imprecation are faith holding on rather than unbelief walking out, and the church's editing of lament from worship has made its speech to God dishonest.
stockPhrases: Here is the line we keep missing.
It is not what you were taught.
This is in the Bible. God did not leave it out.
sold to you by people who could not handle a God big enough to be yelled at
unverifiable: Psalm 44:23 rendered 'Rouse yourself. Why do you sleep, O Lord' is reordered and not ESV verbatim ('Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? Rouse yourself!')
'Let death take them by surprise' (Psalm 55:15) is NIV wording, not ESV ('Let death steal over them')
Psalm 44:11 rendered 'like sheep for the slaughter' (ESV: 'like sheep for slaughter')
'roughly a third of them are laments' (commonly stated, hedged; acceptable as hedged)

essay:when-god-is-silent-and-the-room-is.title: Where Is God When You're Grieving?
essay:when-god-is-silent-and-the-room-is.notes: This is the strongest of the eight: it begins in the room ("The bed is still made on one side"), refuses the explanations after granting them fairly ("Each contains something true... offered today, into this silence, they become cruelty"), and the writer is inside it ("nothing in my hands worth giving," "We are comforting ourselves at their expense"). The ending passes through the tomb and refuses to close the distance ("no sentence I write closes that distance by an inch"). What keeps it from a pass is gait: roughly thirteen "not X / Y" antitheses in 2,400 words ("Not on purpose. By reflex," "I am not handing you that as a fix. I am handing it to you as a fact," "We are not comforting them. We are comforting ourselves"), so the tic outnumbers the genuine hinges (why/where, Saturday, the last line). Two citation slips: Psalm 88's last line is given in NIV wording ("darkness is my closest friend") while the earlier verses are ESV, unmarked; and John of the Cross did not write the Dark Night "from a cell" (composed after the Toledo imprisonment). Cut a third of the antitheses and fix the two references and this ships.

signals.thesis: God's silence in grief is not God's absence but the silence of Holy Saturday, the God who has gone all the way down into the place where the griever now sits.
stockPhrases: Sit with what that means.
unverifiable: "John of the Cross wrote about it from a cell" — the Dark Night was composed after his escape from the Toledo cell, not in it
Psalm 88:18 rendered "darkness is my closest friend" (NIV) while 88:6 and 88:8 are ESV; translation switch unmarked

essay:the-faith-once-delivered.title: What Did Christians Believe Before America Existed?
essay:the-faith-once-delivered.notes: Real thinking and a sound canonical spine (Jude 3, 2 Tim 1:13–14, 2 Thess 2:15 all accurate), but the essay recycles itself: Pelikan's "same trunk growing new rings" appears in two sections, and the sentence "This is why the recovery of the ancient, global faith is not nostalgia and not a retreat into history. It is the discovery that..." is repeated almost verbatim two sections later ("This is why the recovery of the ancient faith is not a retreat into the past. It is the discovery that..."). The nation-fusion turn is never steelmanned — no account of the real goods or wounds that make people bind faith to country — and the indictment stays outward ("it costs the American reader something"; the writer enters only as the convert who rejected the local version, never as someone who did the fusing). Section openers are pure signposting ("Here is the fact that broke my American assumptions," "Now the turn," "Let me tell you what this does"), the antithesis count runs to thirteen, and the ending restates the opening thesis and closes on inspiration ("worth your one short life") rather than through repentance. Wilken is named without a work or idea; remove the name and the sentence says the same thing.

signals.thesis: The Christian faith was settled in its essentials centuries before any modern nation existed, and recovering that fact frees the believer from tying the faith's fate to their country or their moment.
stockPhrases: There is a sentence I want you to sit with
Here is the fact that broke my American assumptions
Now the turn, and it costs the American reader something
Let me tell you what this does to a person
That is the freedom in it.
unverifiable: Robert Louis Wilken "spent his career recovering this" — no work, idea, or text named; decorative attribution
Newbigin "nearly forty years as a missionary in India" — roughly 35–38 years across two stints; acceptable but loose

essay:the-trinity-plainly.title: How Can God Be Three and One?
essay:the-trinity-plainly.notes: The argument accumulates properly — the objection is granted in the writer's own mouth ("I used to make it, loudly, and I had not earned it"), Arius is steelmanned ("It preserved the math beautifully... It was tidy. It was popular"), and the history (325, homoousios, five exiles, the Cappadocian what/who distinction, Sanders 2010) checks out; the Scripture is ESV-accurate. The ending is earned and returns to the objection honestly ("I had been objecting to a cartoon"). But the gait is the old register: fifteen or so hard-period antitheses ("The church did not flunk arithmetic. The church refused to let arithmetic be the measure of God," "Not a transaction. Not a ticket. An adoption," "Love is not something God does. Love is what God eternally is"), plus signposts and a hype turn ("and it changes everything"). Gregory of Nazianzus's One/Three passage (Or. 40.41) is paraphrased twice in different sections, the ocean-and-cup image is used twice, and the "lonely at the center" point is made three times; the piece needs its duplicates cut and its antitheses reduced to the two or three that are actual hinges.

signals.thesis: The Trinity was never an answer to a math problem but the church's refusal to drop either the oneness of God or the full deity of Father, Son, and Spirit, and it finally means that God is love in himself, before anything was made.
stockPhrases: Here is what took me years to see
This is the part newcomers almost never hear, and it changes everything.
Here is why this matters
unverifiable: Gregory of Nazianzus "dance of light" — the essay's own gloss on Oration 40.41, offered as if his image; the underlying passage is real but paraphrased twice

essay:what-the-creed-leaves-out.title: What the Creed Refuses to Argue About
essay:what-the-creed-leaves-out.notes: The cleanest register in the batch — developed paragraphs, a fair two-cliff structure ("the anxious heart" and "the dissolving heart") that indicts both directions with the same instrument, and real sources (Vincent's ubique, semper, ab omnibus; Lewis's hall and rooms rendered faithfully; Pelikan on development). Self-implication is thin but present ("it took me years to feel both edges of it," "I came into this expecting to have to swallow a thousand certainties"), though on the actual charge — promoting opinions to the level of the creed — he only reports having "watched it happen." Three sections open on the same signpost ("So here is something that should surprise you," "Here is why this matters," "And here is the part that should feel like fresh air"), and the closings lean on perfect symmetry ("people with strong convictions and no charity, or people with endless charity and no convictions"; "freer than he feared... more accountable than he hoped"). Romans 14:5 is misquoted ("Let each be fully convinced" is not ESV's "Each one should be fully convinced"), and both Romans 14 and 1 Corinthians 15 are cited without verse numbers. The last paragraph summarizes before it lands its good final line ("The shortness is the mercy").

signals.thesis: The genius of the creeds is their restraint: a small non-negotiable center and a wide field of freedom, and most Christian bitterness comes from losing that line in one direction or the other.
stockPhrases: So here is something that should surprise you
Here is why this matters, and why getting it wrong does real damage.
And here is the part that should feel like fresh air
unverifiable: Romans 14:5 rendered "Let each be fully convinced in his own mind" — ESV reads "Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind"; cited only as "Romans 14"
1 Corinthians 15:14, 19 cited only as "1 Corinthians 15"

essay:why-christians-recite-creeds.title: Why Would Anyone Recite a 1,700-Year-Old Creed?
essay:why-christians-recite-creeds.notes: The objection is given honestly ("it is not stupid"), the NT evidence is accurate (1 Cor 15:3–5 c. 55, 1 Tim 3:16, Jude 3, Deut 6:4 all ESV-correct), Kelly 1950 and Pelikan are real and doing work, and the writer is inside it throughout ("I had spent my unbelieving years convinced I was thinking alone, and bravely"). The ending is earned and personal ("what undid me was not the theology. It was the company"). But there are factual errors a sharp reader will catch: Jude is not "the shortest book in the New Testament" (2 and 3 John are shorter), and "to let the dead vote" is Chesterton's democracy of the dead placed beside Lewis's chronological snobbery as though it were Lewis's. Athanasius spending "most of his adult life on the run" overstates roughly seventeen years of exile. Register-wise it runs on thirteen antitheses ("That is not nothing. That is the opposite of a dead ritual," "That is not weakness. That is the whole design") and signposted turns ("Now the turn that surprised me most," "There is also this"). Fix the Jude and Chesterton errors, thin the antitheses, and it is close.

signals.thesis: A creed is not a substitute for thinking but the costly result of other people's thinking, handed on so the faith need not be rebuilt every Sunday; "just me and my Bible" is the recent and fragile idea, not the creed.
stockPhrases: Picture the strangest thing a modern person can imagine doing in public.
says something that should stop you
Now the turn that surprised me most, the one that costs the modern reader something.
There is also this.
That is not nothing.
unverifiable: "The shortest book in the New Testament... Jude" — false; 2 John and 3 John are shorter
"to let the dead vote... the vote of the dead" attached to C. S. Lewis — this is Chesterton's "democracy of the dead" (Orthodoxy), not Lewis
Arius's songs "sung by dockworkers" — Philostorgius reports songs for sailors, millers, and travelers; "dockworkers" is a gloss
Athanasius "most of his adult life on the run" — about seventeen of forty-five episcopal years in exile

essay:why-the-incarnation-matters.title: Why It Matters That God Became a Baby
essay:why-the-incarnation-matters.notes: The architecture is right (cozy card, the scandal, the Gnostic refusal, Athanasius, Chalcedon 451 with its four adverbs correctly given, the God who knows from inside, the thirty hidden years) and the writer enters as pastor and former atheist ("the thing I, as an atheist, was least prepared for"). The serious problem is the citation of Athanasius's "most quoted line": the essay renders it "so that we might become, not God, but God's," but De Incarnatione 54 says he became man that we might become god (divine); the essay has altered the most famous sentence in the book and presented the alteration as his. The earlier quotation ("having a body that could die, he might die in the place of all, and might restore the corrupt to incorruption") is not verbatim from any standard translation I can confirm, and Hebrews 2:18 is quoted as "being tested" where ESV reads "tempted," cited under a 2:14–18 range for a one-verse quote. "No other religion has ever dared to say this" is an unqualified sweep that avatar traditions would contest. The close performs an anaphoric triplet ("That is God... That is the maker of light... That is the source of all words") and a symmetrical slogan ("The smallness was the strategy. The weakness was the point") on top of eleven antitheses; the Nazareth section duplicates ordinary-time nearly paragraph for paragraph.

signals.thesis: The Incarnation — God taking a real, mortal human body — is the most offensive claim any religion has made, and the offense is precisely the saving part: God entered the flesh to rescue it from inside.
stockPhrases: To feel why this matters, you have to feel why it offended people.
This is where it stops being ancient and becomes yours.
That is the practical payload of an ancient doctrine.
There is one more consequence of the Incarnation that a newcomer rarely hears
unverifiable: Athanasius's "most quoted line" rendered "so that we might become, not God, but God's" — De Incarnatione 54 reads that he became man that we might become god/divine; the essay alters it

Athanasius quotation "in order that, having a body that could die, he might die in the place of all, and might restore the corrupt to incorruption" — not verbatim from a standard translation as far as I can verify
Hebrews 2:18 quoted as "he is able to help those who are being tested" — ESV reads "tempted"; quote of v.14 cited as 2:14–18
C. S. Lewis called the Incarnation the miracle "after which everything else is comment" — cannot verify this phrasing
"No other religion has ever dared to say this, and most have specifically refused to" — unqualified; contestable

essay:easter-is-not-a-day.title: Why Is Easter Fifty Days and Not One Sunday?
essay:easter-is-not-a-day.notes: The proportion argument is genuinely good ("We are rigorous about the fasting and careless about the feast... It is a confession"), the history holds (no kneeling in Eastertide, the eighth day, 1 Cor 15 as the earliest account, Wright 2008), the Scripture is ESV-accurate, and the writer implicates himself concretely ("I have kept Easter as a single Sunday for most of my life, and I can tell you exactly what it produced"). The graveside paragraph carries real pastoral weight. Two failures. First, "Schmemann, again, saw the whole Christian life as fundamentally Paschal" is the first and only mention of Schmemann in the essay — no first name, no work, no prior reference; a paragraph was cut or the piece was stitched, and a reader trips on it. Second, a Baptist pastor commending Eastertide never states the strong case of his own tradition against the church calendar (the Puritan and free-church objection that seasons are unbiblical), so the piece asserts the season rather than earning it against its best objector. Eleven antitheses ("This is not a man surviving his own funeral. This is the hinge of history turning"), paired symmetrical slogans ("The feast was longer than the fast. The joy outlasted the sorrow"), and "cracked... open" used twice in consecutive paragraphs.

signals.thesis: Easter was never a day but a fifty-day season, and the modern church's shrinking of it to one Sunday is a confession of which it finds more believable, its sin or the resurrection.
stockPhrases: Picture a typical Easter.
Here is where the season stops being history and starts making claims on the ordinary Tuesday.
Schmemann, again
unverifiable: "Schmemann, again" — no earlier mention, no first name, no work cited; dangling reference
"We spend more time celebrating the end of a war or the start of a new year than the church historically spent celebrating" — unsupported comparison

essay:ordinary-time.title: What the Boring Middle of the Year Teaches You
essay:ordinary-time.notes: The self-implication is the best thing here and is concrete ("I have spent years measuring my own ministry by the dramatic, the big Sunday, the numbers... I had the proportions backwards"), and the sources are real and correctly dated (Peterson 1980, Warren 2016, Luke 2:52, 1 Thess 4:11, Col 3:17, Zech 4:10 all ESV-accurate). But the essay says one thing a dozen ways: the waiting-room antithesis appears three times ("was not a waiting room before the real life began. It was real life," "The ordinary is not the interruption. The ordinary is the real thing," "is not the waiting room for some more significant life... It is the life"), the closing paragraphs recap in anaphora ("Most of your faithfulness will be invisible. Most of your obedience will go unnoticed. Most of the following of Jesus..."), and the thirty-years-in-Nazareth section duplicates the incarnation essay. No opposing case is stated — the revivalist's real claim that conversion and Acts are dramatic goes unheard — and the smartphone paragraph is stock cultural commentary. Peterson's title is described as "a line about discipleship" when the line is Nietzsche's (Beyond Good and Evil §188), which Peterson borrowed; and the weeping elders belong to Ezra 3:12 and Haggai 2:3, not Zechariah. Stock turns ("Think about that," "a sentence that should stop us cold") and twelve antitheses mark the old gait.

signals.thesis: Ordinary Time, the church year's longest and least dramatic season, is where most of a faithful life is actually lived and formed, and the church was right to give the most weeks to the kind of time we have most of.
stockPhrases: Here is the fact that should reorganize how we think about the unspectacular
Think about that.
a sentence that should stop us cold
unverifiable: Peterson's A Long Obedience "takes its title from a line about discipleship" — the line is Nietzsche's (Beyond Good and Evil §188), which Peterson applied to discipleship
Nazareth "produced a proverb about how nothing good comes out of it" — John 1:46 is Nathanael's remark, not a proverb
The older people "weeping at how small the new beginning is" placed under Zechariah 4 — the weeping is Ezra 3:12 / Haggai 2:3

essay:what-is-advent.title: What Is Advent, and Why Wait for Something That Already Happened?
essay:what-is-advent.notes: This is the mature register working: developed paragraphs, no em-dashes, the argument accumulating from the December ache through the two comings to the genuinely original stretch on hope ('A hope that has already received what it hoped for is no longer hope; it is possession'). Self-implication is concrete and true to biography: 'I have spent Decembers numbing the ache with activity... It was avoidance wearing tinsel,' and 'as someone who came up with no church calendar at all, as I did.' The ending passes through the oldest prayer rather than recapping. Two copyedits before it ships: Isaiah 9:2 is quoted as 'on them has light shined' where ESV reads 'shone' (the rest of the quote is ESV), and 'Here is the piece that resolves the puzzle' is the one signpost I would cut. The five 'Not X. Y.' turns sit at real hinges rather than running as a gait.

signals.thesis: Advent rehearses the first coming in order to train the church to wait for the second, and a culture that has abolished waiting has thereby lost the capacity for hope, which can only exist in the gap before a promise is kept.
stockPhrases: Here is the piece that resolves the puzzle
That kind of hope is a muscle, and like any muscle it atrophies without use
unverifiable: Isaiah 9:2 quoted as 'on them has light shined' — ESV reads 'on them has light shone'; fix or name the translation
Fleming Rutledge 'insists that Advent is the most countercultural season' — paraphrase attributed to Advent (2018), not checked against the page
Bobby Gross, Living the Christian Year — 'inhabit their longing rather than anesthetize it' is paraphrase; wording not verified

essay:why-lent.title: Why Would Anyone Give Something Up for Lent?
essay:why-lent.notes: The thinking is sound and the paragraphs are developed, but the piece runs on the old gait: I count thirteen 'Not X. Y.' constructions ('Giving something up is not the point. It is the method,' 'The fasting is not a transaction. It is a kind of companionship,' 'The mourning is not the destination. It is the door'), and it closes on a fragment antithesis, 'Not to suffer. To get free.' The tic outnumbers the hinge. Self-implication is real and earns its place ('I have avoided this honesty for long stretches of my own life... Comfort is a wonderful place to hide'; 'I include myself and my own ministry in this'). Sources are real and accurately paraphrased — Foster's 'fasting reveals the things that control us' is close to Celebration of Discipline, and Great Lent is correctly dated 1969 — but the wellness paragraph ('juice cleanse and a digital detox') and 'strength training for the soul' are stock, and the triple rhetorical question opening the last section is a machine turn. Cut the antithesis by two-thirds and rebuild the close as a sentence and it passes.

signals.thesis: Lent removes the comforts that numb a person not to prove willpower but to expose what those comforts were covering, walking with Jesus into the wilderness where repentance turns out to be a gift and the fruit is freedom from one's own appetites.
stockPhrases: Start with the misunderstanding, because nearly everyone holds it
It is strength training for the soul
juice cleanse and a digital detox
So why would anyone do this? Why choose discomfort in a world engineered to eliminate it? Why give something up when...
Not to suffer. To get free.
unverifiable: Schmemann, Great Lent — 'The fasting, he wrote, is meant to bring us back to a hunger deeper than food' is reported as 'he wrote' without page; treat as paraphrase and mark it so
James 4:8–9 quoted with 'you double-minded' silently omitted between 'purify your hearts' and 'Be wretched' — add an ellipsis or restore

essay:why-the-church-has-a-calendar.title: Why Does the Church Have Its Own Calendar?
essay:why-the-church-has-a-calendar.notes: Competent argument, correct against the old rules, wrong against the current voice: roughly sixteen 'Not X. Y.' constructions carry the essay ('The retail year is not neutral. It is a discipleship program,' 'What the church calendar offers is not intensity. It is duration,' 'The Christian year is not a loop. It is a story told in a circle'), plus a three-part anaphora ('You do not read about waiting in Advent. You wait. You do not study repentance in Lent. You repent...'). Signposts pile up: 'Hear what that means,' 'Now stand back and see what you are looking at,' 'Here is what I missed for years.' The self-implication is honest ('I have caught my own attention organized around the next purchase... while the death and resurrection of the Son of God sat somewhere on a shelf'). The ending restates the opening line ('Everyone keeps a calendar. The only question is whose' becomes 'Whose time are you keeping. You are keeping someone's. You always were') — a symmetrical recap with a sting, not a verdict the argument arrived at. The Smith citation is specific and does work; the Webber line and the second-century 'small public treason' claim are gestured rather than grounded.

signals.thesis: The Christian year is a rival calendar that forms people by repetition into the story of Jesus, against a consumer calendar that forms them into perpetual wanting; there is no neutral year, only the question of whose story shapes your time.
stockPhrases: Hear what that means.
Now stand back and see what you are looking at.
Here is what I missed for years.
That is surrender with the lights off.
This is its quiet genius and its hardest sell.
unverifiable: Robert Webber — 'the Christian year, he wrote, is a way of ordering all of life around the central truth that Jesus is Lord of time itself' — no title given, wording not verified (Ancient-Future Time is the likely source)
Schmemann, For the Life of the World — the paraphrase on the liturgical year 'entering' events is not checked against the text
'The early Christians... refused to mark the imperial holy days' / 'a believer in the second century' — no event, source, or figure named; vague history presented as history

essay:the-table-that-divides.title: Why Does Communion Divide Churches Instead of Uniting?
essay:the-table-that-divides.notes: The strongest piece in the batch: it starts at Corinth rather than the proximate cause, steelmans closed Communion in a form its defenders would sign ('It is, in their own understanding, integrity... They take the table so seriously that they will not cheapen it with a unity they have not actually reached'), refuses the cheap fix ('The answer to a divided table is not a meaningless one'), and ends through cross and marriage supper. It is one short repair from passing. 'Sit with that.' is the stock 'let that sink in' turn and cannot ship; 'staggering' appears twice in adjacent sections. The self-implication lives in 'we' ('We did not invent this sin. We inherited it and gave it new forms') but never reaches 'I' at the paragraph where it would cost something — 'Sunday morning remains... the most segregated hour' is written about churches in general by a pastor who has one. All Scripture is quoted in NIV without naming it, against the house ESV default; the quotes are accurate to NIV.

signals.thesis: The Lord's Supper was given as the sign and engine of the church's unity, and the church has made it the clearest evidence of its division; the honest doctrinal divisions deserve respect but must still be grieved, and the divisions with no doctrinal warrant, by race and class, are the Corinthian sin in Sunday clothes.
stockPhrases: Sit with that.
Here is the deepest thing, and it is the one Scripture forces.
raw honesty
staggering (used twice)
unverifiable: Newbigin 'had watched mission fields where the gospel was preached by people who could not share Communion with one another' — no text named; his ecumenical writing supports the gist but the specific claim is unsourced
1 Corinthians 11:17–22, 10:17, John 17:21, Galatians 2:11–14 quoted in NIV without naming the translation (house default is ESV)
'the most segregated hour' — King's line, unattributed

essay:what-happens-at-communion.title: What Actually Happens at Communion?
essay:what-happens-at-communion.notes: This is the contested-doctrine protocol done properly: Rome, Orthodoxy, Luther, Zwingli, and Calvin each stated in a form their own would recognize ('Calvin thought Zwingli had made the meal too thin... and that Rome had made it too crude'), then the shared ground named before any weighing. The prose is calm and spoken — 'nobody fights this long over a snack,' 'I would rather belong to a church that argued for centuries about what happens at this table than one that found the question too small to bother with.' The first-person testimony is concrete and true to a working pastor ('I have given that bread to people on the worst day of their lives and watched something steady them that I did not put there'), and the ending returns to the line forming without recapping. Two notes that do not change the verdict: the author never names where he himself lands, which the scholarship standard asks for after the steelman, and all Scripture is NIV unnamed. Augustine's 'Be what you can see, and receive what you are' (Sermon 272) and Schmemann's 1963 date check out.

signals.thesis: Christians have disagreed for two millennia about what 'is' means in 'this is my body,' but every tradition agrees that Christ meets his people at the table, and the ferocity of the disagreement is itself evidence that something happens there rather than something merely remembered.
stockPhrases: Now the hard question, the one the centuries fought over.
So set them side by side.
But here is what no one in that line is doing.
unverifiable: 1 Corinthians 11:23–26, 10:16–17, John 6:51 quoted in NIV without naming the translation (house default is ESV)
Luther 'in, with, and under' — standard Lutheran shorthand (Formula of Concord), not Luther's verbatim phrase; fine as tradition but not as a quote

essay:why-baptism.title: What Baptism Is Actually For
essay:why-baptism.notes: The thinking is good and the believer's/infant steelman is exemplary ('it is not the lazy tradition its critics sometimes assume... The baby contributes nothing. That, he thought, is the whole point of grace'), with the author naming his own landing and its limits. But the scaffolding is sermon-outline language the standard names to avoid — 'The first surprise,' 'The second surprise,' 'The third surprise' — and the prose leans on nine 'Not X. Y.' turns plus tweet-length verdicts ('Nobody got baptized for the photo,' 'Get that straight and the rest steadies'). The one swipe is at people, not a position: '"Spiritual but not religious" is, at bottom, a preference for a faith with no witnesses.' The writer positions himself ('the tradition I serve in') but never enters the indictment; 'We are the most privately spiritual generation that has ever lived' is where a man who came to faith from outside the church should have said what he wanted. The Large Catechism quotation and the 'baptizatus sum' night anecdote need sourcing; N. T. Wright's 'passport' summary names no text and the sentence says the same thing without him.

signals.thesis: Baptism is not the church marking a person's decision but God's act done to the person — a burial and raising, a public entrance into a people — which is why it can steady a believer on the nights his own faith cannot.
stockPhrases: The first surprise / The second surprise / The third surprise
Nobody got baptized for the photo.
Strip it back to the center.
Get that straight and the rest steadies.
Here is where a newcomer's instinct usually points the wrong way.
unverifiable: Luther, Large Catechism (1529): baptism 'is not our work but God's' — presented in quotation marks; the Catechism says God's act though performed by human hands, but this exact wording is not verified

Luther steadying himself 'in the middle of the night' with 'baptizatus sum' — widely repeated tradition (the Wartburg anecdote), no primary source given; also the Latin is two words, the essay says 'three words'
N. T. Wright 'has spent much of his career arguing' baptism was 'the closest thing the early church had to a passport' — no text named; decoration by the remove-the-name test
'They built baptisteries shaped like tombs and shaped like wombs' — unsourced (Cyril of Jerusalem's font-as-tomb-and-mother would ground it)
Romans 6:3–4, Colossians 2:12, Acts 2:38–39, Matthew 28:19 quoted in NIV without naming the translation

essay:why-christians-confess-out-loud.title: Why Christians Confess Their Sins Out Loud
essay:why-christians-confess-out-loud.notes: Strong diagnosis and the Bonhoeffer material is real and doing work ('He who is alone with his sin is utterly alone'; the 'breakthrough' language is Life Together's own). The traditions are treated fairly ('The Catholic guards the certainty of the spoken word. The Protestant guards its availability to every believer'). The failure is that an essay about saying your worst out loud contains no 'I' anywhere: it is 'we,' 'you,' and 'the person who has confessed' from first line to last, and the freedom section ('There is a particular relief that exists only on the far side of being fully known') is exactly where a pastor who hears these confessions, and makes them, should have entered. Eleven 'Not X. Y.' constructions cluster toward the end ('not a museum of the righteous but a hospital for the honest,' 'not just a listener, but a word back. Not only the relief... but the verdict'). One factual correction: Life Together was written in 1938 after the Gestapo closed Finkenwalde in 1937 and published in 1939; 'wrote Life Together in 1939 from inside an underground seminary' has the sequence wrong.

signals.thesis: Secrets grow in the dark and own the person keeping them, and the only thing that breaks their power is saying them aloud to someone who does not leave; absolution exists because forgiveness has to become audible before it becomes real.
stockPhrases: Start with the diagnosis, because confession only makes sense once you see the disease.
It is worth clearing away two misunderstandings
That gets it precisely backward.
The word does the work. The feelings follow when they follow.
unverifiable: Bonhoeffer 'wrote Life Together in 1939 from inside an underground seminary the Nazi state had outlawed' — Finkenwalde was closed in 1937 and the book was written in 1938 (published 1939); the setting as stated is inaccurate

Augustine, Confessions — 'You were within me, and I was in the world outside myself' presented as a quotation; Book X.27 reads 'you were within and I was outside' in standard translations; name the translation or render as paraphrase
Psalm 32:3–5, James 5:16, John 20:23, 1 John 1:9 quoted in NIV without naming the translation

essay:why-faith-uses-physical-things.title: Why Christianity Uses Bread, Water, and Wine
essay:why-faith-uses-physical-things.notes: Sound argument, and the section on the modern split ('a vast meaningless universe of atoms out there, and a small fragile theater of significance in here') is the essay's real contribution — but it is the most old-register piece of the eight. I count more than twenty 'Not X. Y.' constructions; nearly every paragraph closes on one ('The physical thing is not a metaphor... The physical thing is the means,' 'It is not higher than the sacramental faith. It is thinner,' 'It says the cosmos was never meaningless. It was always gift'), alongside machine-symmetrical triplets ('Water that washes. Bread that feeds. Oil that heals'; 'The water really wets you. The bread really feeds you. The hand really rests on your shoulder'). The writer never appears, which is a loss here more than anywhere: the paragraph on the West learning 'to treat the physical universe as inert' is a former atheist's own story, and he does not tell it. That same paragraph opens 'Somewhere along the way the West learned' — vague claims presented as history, no date, no Taylor. The Mark 14:22 quotation does not match Mark in ESV or NIV. The close ('He invented matter. He has never once been ashamed of it') restates Lewis and the thesis in four short sentences. The fix is pervasive but sentence-level; the thinking stays.

signals.thesis: Christianity treats matter as something God made, called good, entered in the Incarnation, and is redeeming, so bread, water, and oil are not props of a primitive religion but the places God has chosen to be met, against both the ancient Gnostic and the modern instinct to treat the physical as lower.
stockPhrases: That gets it exactly backward, and the backwardness matters.
So the next time you watch the church do its strange, physical things
Water that washes. Bread that feeds. Oil that heals.
The water really wets you. The bread really feeds you. The hand really rests on your shoulder.
Somewhere along the way the West learned
unverifiable: Mark 14:22 quoted as 'He took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, saying, "This is my body"' — matches neither ESV ('after blessing it broke it and gave it to them, and said, "Take; this is my body"') nor NIV; wording is closer to Luke 22:19 / 1 Corinthians 11:24
C. S. Lewis 'God likes matter. He invented it.' — Mere Christianity reads 'He likes matter. He invented it.' with God as antecedent; acceptable compression but not verbatim as punctuated
'Somewhere along the way the West learned to treat the physical universe as inert' — no date, event, or source for the disenchantment claim
John 1:14 and 1 Timothy 4:4 quoted in NIV without naming the translation

essay:a-day-of-doing-nothing.title: Why a Day of Doing Nothing Is an Act of Defiance
essay:a-day-of-doing-nothing.notes: The Exodus/Deuteronomy distinction, the Brueggemann leveling paragraph ('A people who stop together cannot be ranked by their productivity'), and the Hebrews 4 turn are real accumulation, and the paragraph-two self-implication ('I was afraid of who I would be if I stopped') is concrete and in role as a working pastor. What keeps it from shipping is the gait: it opens on a staged hook ('Picture telling your most ambitious friend... Watch the discomfort flicker across the face... The discomfort is the tell') and a fragment stack ('Not rest in order to work better. Not recharge for the sake of productivity. Nothing, no email, no errands...'), then runs about seven hard-period antitheses ('Sabbath is not a break from the rat race... Sabbath is the refusal', 'It does not ask the productivity machine for a little less. It stops the machine') as the default connector rather than at hinges. Em-dashes look to have been swapped for commas, leaving run-on chains ('one full day, given over to no purpose that could be written on a resume'). The Comer paragraph is decoration ('has made a career of saying this') with no title; cite it or cut it. Closest of the devotional set to a pass; the fix is the opener and thinning the antithesis.

signals.thesis: Sabbath is not rest so you can work better; it is a weekly act of defiance declaring that a human being's worth was never his output, grounded in Deuteronomy's slavery reasoning and Hebrews' rest from works.
stockPhrases: The discomfort is the tell.
Picture telling your most ambitious friend
reforms a person from the inside out
Not rest in order to work better. Not recharge for the sake of productivity.
unverifiable: Brueggemann 'what he calls the system of anxious productivity' — presented as his phrase; exact wording not confirmed against the text (book, date, and argument are real)
John Mark Comer cited without a title; the claim is generic enough to be decoration

essay:praying-at-fixed-hours.title: What Is Fixed-Hour Prayer and Why Did the Church Keep It?
essay:praying-at-fixed-hours.notes: The Scripture spine does real work and reads correctly against ESV wording (Psalm 119:164, Psalm 55:17, Daniel 6:10, Acts 3:1), the Daniel paragraph ('They threatened a structure he had built in peacetime, brick by ordinary brick') is the essay's best writing, and the Reformers get a fair hearing ('So much of what they recovered was pure gain'). But the old register is the gait: anaphora stacks ('Not the harvest. Not the guests. Not the mood of the man kneeling down.'; 'Prayer with a clock. Prayer with a script. Prayer that starts at noon because it is noon.') and about nine hard-period antitheses ('The schedule was not the enemy of real prayer. The schedule was the thing...', 'The hard part is not the content. The hard part is the obedience'). Two factual problems: 'three centuries later we are living in the wreckage of that overcorrection' undercounts the distance from the Reformers by two hundred years, and 'Read that as a literal count, because that is how the people who first sang it read it' asserts an ancient reading of Psalm 119:164 the essay cannot show (seven as completeness is at least as common). The ending is earned; it closes the loop on the waiting-room opener without restating the thesis.

signals.thesis: Prayer anchored to the clock rather than the mood is what keeps prayer alive when feeling runs out, and recovering the daily office is the most quietly radical thing a distracted modern Christian could do.
stockPhrases: Be honest about it.
the most countercultural minute of your workday
She was describing us.
Do it anyway.
unverifiable: 'that is how the people who first sang it read it' (Psalm 119:164 as a literal seven) — no source; the symbolic reading is common
'three centuries later' after the Reformers — arithmetic is wrong; it is five
Eugene Peterson's argument summarized without a title (Answering God, 1989, would carry it); no quotation invented

essay:reading-the-bible-slowly.title: How to Read the Bible Slowly, the Old Way
essay:reading-the-bible-slowly.notes: The self-implication is the strongest in the devotional set and specific to a working pastor ('I had turned the living word into a database, and a database does not change you'), and Peterson's Eat This Book (2006) and Guigo II's four rungs are real and correctly described. The failure is the tic count: about eleven 'Not X. Y.' pairs ('You are not trying to cover ground. You are taking a small thing in.', 'Coverage is not communion.', 'The Bible was never meant to be gotten through. It was meant to be eaten.') plus the formation-versus-information antithesis repeated until it is a slogan ('formation instead of information', 'The first leaves you the manager of the material. The second makes you the disciple of a voice.'). The close is a recap: the last paragraph re-says the bolded thesis (eaten, voice, listening) after an imperative stack ('Read them again. Notice the word that catches. Stay with it. Turn it into a prayer.'). Joshua 1:8 is misquoted ('shall not depart out of your mouth' is KJV wording; ESV reads 'from your mouth'). Cut the slogan repetitions, fix the verse, and find an ending that advances rather than restates.

signals.thesis: Scripture asks to be eaten, not skimmed; slow reading in the lectio divina pattern is the only kind that forms a soul, while extraction-reading leaves the reader unchanged.
stockPhrases: naming it is half the cure
it is the trained reflex, and it is lying to you
Coverage is not communion.
formation instead of information
unverifiable: Joshua 1:8 'depart out of your mouth' — ESV reads 'depart from your mouth'; minor misquote
Guigo II 'around the year 1150' — the Scala Claustralium is usually placed later in the twelfth century; approximate
Guigo's four-part eating image is paraphrased loosely ('prayer asks for what the chewing revealed you needed'); the original has prayer extracting the flavor

essay:silence-and-solitude.title: What the Desert Fathers Knew About Silence
essay:silence-and-solitude.notes: The Abba Moses material (the cell saying, the basket of sand) and Nouwen's 'furnace of transformation' are real and used as witnesses rather than decoration, and the second self-implication ('This is the part of the indictment I have to include myself in, because I carry the same device') lands where it should. The register fails on density: about twelve antitheses ('Solitude is not where you go to get away from your problems. It is where you go to finally have them', 'The cell did not make him cold. It made him kind', 'The discomfort is not a sign that it is not working. The discomfort is the work.') and perfectly symmetrical triplets ('The notification is engineered to interrupt. The feed is engineered never to end. The autoplay is engineered...', 'Sit still. Stay put. Stop running.'). The Willard hurry line reaches us secondhand through Ortberg, and the essay extends it ('not sin in the obvious sense but hurry, and hurry's faithful companion, noise') beyond what was reported. The ending is earned ('hard mercy... hand you back to yourself and to God'), though it too closes on an anaphora pair ('It will not entertain you. It will not flatter you.').

signals.thesis: Solitude, as the desert fathers practiced it, is not an escape but the furnace where a person finally faces himself and God without the noise, and our noise is manufactured on purpose.
stockPhrases: Try this and see what happens.
we are not its customers so much as its harvest
The discomfort is the work.
The notification is engineered to interrupt. The feed is engineered never to end.
unverifiable: Dallas Willard on hurry as the great enemy of the spiritual life — known secondhand via John Ortberg; the 'not sin... and noise' extension is the essay's own
1 Kings 19:12 'the sound of thin silence' — a literal rendering, not ESV; fine if marked as such

essay:why-christians-fast.title: Why Christians Fast (and Why You Probably Stopped)
essay:why-christians-fast.notes: The most honestly self-implicated of the set ('it is aimed straight at people like me'; 'it implicates me as much as anyone'), the Isaiah 58 turn toward the neighbor keeps the discipline from curdling into self-improvement, and the Protestant recoil is steelmanned ('That fear is not groundless'). The Scripture reads correctly against ESV wording (Matthew 6:16-18, 4:4, Joel 2:12, Isaiah 58:6-7), and Foster's line about fasting revealing what controls us is faithfully paraphrased. The register still runs on antithesis, about ten ('He is not despising bread. He is locating it.', 'Fasting does not create those disorders. It uncovers them'), plus a fragment triplet ('The anger we suppress with a snack. The anxiety we mute with a meal. The restlessness we feed...') and 'When you fast. Not if.' 'Training, not trying' is Ortberg's phrasing of Willard rather than Willard's, and 'went out with the dishwater' mangles the idiom. Trim the pairs and it ships.

signals.thesis: Fasting is voluntary hunger that exposes how our appetites run us and reorders them toward the hunger we were made for; the church stopped fasting because it stopped believing its appetites were disordered.
stockPhrases: There is a question worth sitting with before anything else.
Hungry: the food arrives. Bored: the screen lights up.
worth sitting with
raise a household of tyrants
unverifiable: 'work by training, not by trying' attributed to Willard — the formulation is John Ortberg's popularization; Willard's athlete analogy is real
'went out with the dishwater' — idiom error, not a citation issue

essay:did-the-resurrection-happen.title: Did the Resurrection Actually Happen?
essay:did-the-resurrection-happen.notes: The architecture is right for a skeptic: it starts with what the field concedes, dates the 1 Corinthians 15 creed early, gives Wright's novelty argument, and the Hume section is the essay's real contribution because it is self-implicated ('I held that as an axiom. I no longer think it is reasoning; I think it is a decision dressed as reasoning'). The ending is earned and refuses the altar call ('it would not stay closed'). But the register is the old one: 'Not a proof. Not a knockdown.', 'Had hoped. Past tense.', 'Go ask them.', and about fourteen antitheses ('That last clause is not the language of legend. It is the language of a man inviting verification'), and the alternatives section is a perfectly symmetrical 'Maybe... But...' triad that dispatches each rival in a paragraph. Fairness is partial: 'hallucinations... do not happen to five hundred people at once' asserts the disputed point (the five hundred exist only in Paul's list), 'not in serious dispute' overstates consensus on the empty tomb, and the strongest current skeptical account (Ehrman's late-tomb-tradition reading) is never named though 'serious people' are gestured at. The 1 Corinthians 15:14 citation carries paraphrase drawn from verses 15 and 19.

signals.thesis: The resurrection is the best available historical explanation of facts most scholars, skeptical ones included, already grant; not a proof, but the rival explanations each rescue one corner of the evidence and leave the rest exposed.
stockPhrases: Not a proof. Not a knockdown.
Go ask them.
Had hoped. Past tense.
Nobody, nobody, was expecting
unverifiable: 1 Corinthians 15:14 cited for 'liars who should be pitied' — that content is vv.15 and 19; paraphrase under a single-verse reference
'not in serious dispute' for the whole minimal-facts list — the empty tomb and the five hundred are disputed; Habermas himself treats the tomb as short of consensus
Luke 24:11 lēros as 'the babbling of the delirious' — a medical-Greek sense exists, but this is decorative Greek

essay:faith-and-science.title: Do You Have to Choose Between Faith and Science?
essay:faith-and-science.notes: The history is real and dated (Draper 1874, White 1896), the concessions are specific ('The fight over Darwin was real, and parts of the church handled it badly, and parts of the church handle it badly still'), the multiverse gets a fair sentence before the counter, and the former-atheist self-implication is precise ('I had quietly exempted the values I liked from the standard I was using to dismiss the God I did not want'). The ending is earned and leaves the question open. Two register failures: the honesty announcement is repeated mechanically ('I want to be fair', 'I am not claiming', 'I am not papering over those', 'I am not going to pretend', 'I want to be careful not to overclaim') where the standard allows the turn once, and about fourteen antitheses run as the connector ('That is not a defect in the instrument. It is the boundary', 'That is not skepticism. It is selective skepticism'). Sources need tightening: Kepler 'thinking God's thoughts after him' is a popular attribution with no firm primary text, 'Surveys of working scientists consistently turn up' names no survey, and McGrath 'has written extensively' with no title is close to decoration even though the credential is doing argumentative work.

signals.thesis: The faith-science war is a nineteenth-century story (Draper 1874, White 1896), not a finding of science; science grew up among believers, serious scientists still believe, and the question that remains is one science by design cannot answer.
stockPhrases: I want to be fair
I want to be careful not to overclaim
So here is where I land
I am not papering over those
unverifiable: Kepler 'described his astronomy as thinking God's thoughts after him' — widely repeated, no firm primary source
'Surveys of working scientists consistently turn up a sizable minority' — no survey named (Pew 2009 would support it)
'Newton wrote more on theology than on physics' — commonly stated, roughly true by manuscript volume, unsourced here
McGrath's work dismantling the conflict thesis — real, but no title given

essay:if-god-is-good-why-suffering.title: If God Is Good, Why Is There So Much Suffering?
essay:if-god-is-good-why-suffering.notes: The strongest essay in the batch: Ivan's ticket is given at full power and correctly marked as paraphrase ('Ivan says in effect'), Plantinga's limit is stated honestly ('It does not touch the earthquake, the cancer in a child'), Lewis's two books are set against each other without being resolved, the Job reading does theological work, and the ending passes through the cross without generic hope ('They come back saying they are not alone in it. That is less than you wanted. It may be more than you expected.'). The failure is a mannerism: honesty is announced about eight times rather than enacted ('I will not start this one by being clever', 'I refuse to do that', 'I am not going to pretend', 'I am not going to tie a bow on this. There is no bow.', 'I am not going to end this with a resolution'), and two signposts ('Here is where I have to disappoint anyone hoping for the knockout', 'Here is the most I can honestly say') are the stock turn the standard names. Antithesis still runs at about thirteen, though more of these sit at real hinges ('It reads at first like evasion. It is not.') than anywhere else in the batch. Cut six of the eight disclaimers and this ships.

signals.thesis: Suffering does not disprove God (the logical argument collapsed and the moral argument borrows a moral law atheism cannot supply), but it is not explained away either; Christianity offers not a theodicy but a God who entered the suffering.
stockPhrases: Here is where I have to disappoint anyone hoping for the knockout
Here is the most I can honestly say.
I am not going to tie a bow on this. There is no bow.
Press the point one turn further
unverifiable: 'almost no one now argues it is not' possible (Plantinga's free-will scenario) — broadly true (Mackie conceded), but stated as consensus without a source
'one of them I have watched people die holding' — pastoral experience, plausible for a working pastor, not checkable

essay:was-jesus-just-a-good-teacher.title: Was Jesus Really Just a Good Teacher?
essay:was-jesus-just-a-good-teacher.notes: The architecture is the closest to the mature register in this batch: it states Lewis, then pushes on him "harder than most defenders do," gives legend, category, and pluralist objections real room, and the self-implication is genuine ("for years it was mine" ... "I had filed him under great teachers, which is the file you keep things in when you want to honor them without obeying them"). Two things stop it shipping as it stands. The Lewis paragraph contains a broken sentence ("The teacher who also tells you that he can forgive your sins ... that man is not handing you ethics") and the essay is riddled with comma splices where connectors have gone missing ("the trilemma, liar, lunatic, or Lord, has at least two real holes"; "feel light by comparison, it is light because"), and two consecutive paragraphs open "N.T. Wright has argued the same" / "N.T. Wright has added a dimension," which reads as an unmerged draft. The antithesis count (about eight, e.g. "The high claim is not a late verbal addition. It is the earliest layer's account") is roughly one per movement and tolerable, but the lunatic-option paragraph leans on an unsupported psychiatric generalization ("Clinical grandiosity of that order does not generally coexist with") that a skeptic would rightly refuse. The ending ("*Who do you say that I am.* He is still standing there") is earned and leaves weight.

signals.thesis: The polite verdict that Jesus was a great moral teacher and nothing more is the one position the historical evidence makes hardest to hold, because the admired teaching and the divine claims come from the same mouth in the earliest, most Jewish, most securely dated layers, and the legend theory that would separate them has run out of time.
stockPhrases: Here is what I will argue
unverifiable: "Clinical grandiosity of that order does not generally coexist with the teaching attributed to Jesus" — an armchair clinical claim with no source
"for a long stretch of the twentieth century, the mainstream scholarly default" — true in outline but no scholar or work named (Bousset/Bultmann would anchor it)

essay:why-trust-the-bible.title: Why Would Anyone Trust the Bible?
essay:why-trust-the-bible.notes: This is the strongest self-implication in the batch and it is structural, not decorative: "It was load-bearing for my unbelief," and the close, "I had simply transferred my faith from the Bible to the secular folklore about the Bible, and never noticed I had believed something on worse evidence than the thing I was rejecting," is a real verdict against the writer. The contradictions section is fair before it is sharp ("the glib Christian answers to it are genuinely bad") and Bruce, Bauckham, the Pilate inscription, and the criterion of embarrassment are real and doing work. It fails the mature standard in two places: the canon section asserts "The canon was not decided by decree. It emerged by recognition" with no council, no date, no Muratorian fragment, no Athanasius 367, which is exactly the vague-history the voice document forbids; and form criticism is dismissed as "scholarly fashion" without a named opponent (Ehrman never appears) so the strongest skeptic is not in the room. Mechanically the text as given carries comma splices ("if the whole thing was a power grab, you can dismiss it"; "the credulous option, I had simply transferred") that must be resolved before it ships. Antithesis runs about nine ("It is a good plot. It is not history." / "The book is not asking to be trusted blindly. It is asking to be opened."), one per movement and near the line; the closing question is self-implicating rather than engagement bait, and the ending is earned.

signals.thesis: The popular case against the Bible rests on folklore about the Bible (the telephone game, a conspiring council, fatal contradictions) that the scholarship, much of it non-Christian, does not support; clearing it does not prove the book true but removes the excuse the writer himself once leaned on.
stockPhrases: Here is what I will argue
here is what serious historians notice
does not survive contact with
unverifiable: Canon section names no council, date, or document ("The canon was not decided by decree") — the history is gestured at, not given
"The titles Luke gives to local officials ... turned out to be precisely correct" — real (politarchs at Thessalonica) but no example or source given
"God-breathed" for 2 Timothy 3:16 is the NIV rendering, not ESV ("breathed out by God"); translation not named

essay:does-god-change-his-mind.title: Does God Change His Mind?
essay:does-god-change-his-mind.notes: The argument accumulates properly: it names the resistance ("we hear it as unresponsiveness"), runs the opposite out ("If He can change, then His promise to you is a mood, and moods pass"), brings Aquinas and Boethius in to explain a mechanism rather than to decorate, and pastors the doctrine to "the worst night of your life." Where it fails the current register is density: roughly ten hard antitheses ("You are not changing God's mind. You are taking the place"; "The fixed point did not move. The fixed point came near"; "Irrevocable. Not subject to revision. Not a mood"), plus "Let me name the resistance first" and "Let me put the whole thing where it lands" as signposts. The open-theism steelman is real but anonymous ("Some thoughtful Christians have argued in the last few decades") and is not sorted by order before it is answered; its defenders would not sign "a God who is still learning." The "What remains" section opens with a recap paragraph ("God does not change His mind, and God relents. Both are true") that should go, though the final line ("the only thing I have found that holds") is earned through the incarnation section, which is the best writing in the piece.

signals.thesis: God does not change because He is complete rather than rigid, so the verses where He "relents" describe an unchanging mercy meeting a moving world as seen from inside time, and that immutability, carried all the way into the incarnation, is the only love a frightened person can lean on.
stockPhrases: Here is the claim
Let me name the resistance first
Let me put the whole thing where it lands
the worst night of your life
sledgehammer
unverifiable: "the way Boethius's watchman observes the road" — the Consolation (V.6) uses the high watchtower of providence and the man-walking example; the travelers-on-the-road detail is an elaboration, not Boethius
"The theologians have a useful phrase: God is immutable in His character and His purposes, not static in His relationships" — presented as a quoted phrase with no theologian named

essay:is-god-angry.title: Is God Angry?
essay:is-god-angry.notes: The thinking is sound and the self-implication is unusually honest ("You can be an atheist and still be afraid of God. I was"; "I rejected a God who had already been edited down by the very culture I thought I was rebelling against"), and Heschel, Bellah, Nahum, and Volf are witnesses that advance the diagnosis. But this is the old gait wearing full paragraphs: roughly twenty antitheses, one closing nearly every paragraph ("The cartoon God throws lightning. The God of the cross steps in front of it"; "Your sin was not minimized. It was carried"; "The God you were afraid of would have made you pay. The God of the Bible paid"), and the finale stacks them three deep ("That is not a God to manage. That is not a fuse to avoid tripping. That is a love with fire in it"). The only opponent is a "cartoon"; the serious objection to wrath and penal substitution as its defenders would state it is never on the page. Citations need repair: D. A. Carson is Canadian, not "The British scholar"; the Volf recollection about finding wrath "distasteful" until the war appears to come from *Free of Charge* (2005), not *Exclusion and Embrace*; the Heschel fragment in quotation marks could not be verified as his wording; Numbers 23:19 ESV reads "God is not man," not "not a man." Heaviest revise in the batch; the ending is earned but arrives through the tic.

signals.thesis: God's wrath is not the opposite of His love but a function of it, His settled opposition to whatever destroys what He loves, and the cross is where that opposition is borne by God Himself rather than denied.
stockPhrases: So let me say the hard thing plainly
Here is the turn that changed everything for me
Let me give you the working definition
Here is what the cross does to that fear, and it is the whole point
the 3 a.m. dread

Volf, *Exclusion and Embrace* (1996): the "used to find the idea of a wrathful God distasteful ... came to seem not noble but obscene" recollection appears to be from *Free of Charge* (2005); only the nonviolence-requires-divine-judgment thesis is from *Exclusion and Embrace*
Heschel: "'The God of the philosophers,' he wrote, is unmoved" — quoted fragment not verified as Heschel's wording; his contrast is with the God of Aristotle

essay:is-god-in-control.title: If God Is in Control, Why Doesn't It Feel Like It?
essay:is-god-in-control.notes: The pastoral frame is right and the movement from the funeral sentence through Acts 2:23 and Genesis 50:20 to Calvin at three in the morning genuinely accumulates; the reading of Joseph ("two distinct intentions ran through the same event") and the fatalism/providence distinction are the mature register at work. The self-implication is thin: "I have probably said it when I should have said nothing" is the only entry, and the indictment otherwise lands on the people who say the sentence. Sovereignty and freedom is a named contested doctrine and the essay treats "the classical doctrine of providence" as the settled third thing without stating the Arminian or open position in a form its defenders would sign, or naming the order. Antithesis runs about thirteen ("The promise is not that the cancer is good. The promise is that the cancer has not slipped God's grip"; "Not because the dangers are smaller. Because the dangers are not unsupervised"; "You will not always feel the control. You were never promised the feeling"), past one per movement. The Calvin phrase "miserably disquieted" and the Boethius watchman-with-travelers image need checking against the texts; the ending ("the empty tomb did not feel like it either, the morning before they found it open") is earned through the resurrection.

signals.thesis: To say God is sovereign is not to say every event is good or that He authored the evil, but that no event, including the worst one in your life, has escaped His reach or defeated His purpose, as the cross proves.
stockPhrases: The honest thing is this.
at three in the morning
bumper sticker
if you could see the spreadsheet
unverifiable: Calvin, *Institutes* (1559), "miserably disquieted" — could not verify the exact quoted wording; the sense is in I.17.10–11

Boethius "watchman on the hill" with travelers already passed and still coming — the Consolation V.6 uses the watchtower of providence and the man-walking example; the road-and-travelers detail is a reconstruction presented as his picture

essay:the-god-who-hides.title: Why Does God Hide?
essay:the-god-who-hides.notes: The opening states the skeptic's case at full strength ("a perfect, all-loving being who craves relationship but cannot manage to show His face fails his own job description") and the essay stays with the controlling image long enough for it to work, moving canonically from Psalm 13 through Job and Isaiah 45:15 to Luther's cross and John's dark night; the self-implication is concrete without invented biography ("I have prayed into that silence, on ordinary mornings and on a few mornings that were not ordinary at all"). The failures are fixable. Jesus on the cross is said to be "crying His own version of Psalm 13" when the cry is Psalm 22:1 verbatim; Isaiah 45:15 drops ESV's "the Savior"; Luther's Heidelberg Disputation (1518) goes undated in an essay that otherwise dates its witnesses. The "modern church, which trades almost entirely in feelings" is pointed at from outside by a working pastor who should have said "our churches, mine included." About twelve antitheses ("The dark night is not God going away. It is God maturing a love"; "The experience has not changed. The room it happens in has"), and the skeptic's obvious counter to the "visible God would be worse" section (Thomas, Paul, and Moses were shown and not flattened) is never met. The ending is earned but its last line, "People have met Him in that exact question before," softens toward generic reassurance.

signals.thesis: The hiddenness of God is not a flaw the believer tolerates but a theme Scripture and the tradition have prayed through for three thousand years, and it is located finally at the cross, where the absence and presence of God are the same event seen from two sides.
stockPhrases: cosmic vending machine
hidden in plain sight
The ceiling holds (used four times)
